tamil:
அகழ்வாரைத் தாங்கும் நிலம்போலத் தம்மை
இகழ்வார்ப் பொறுத்தல் தலை.
transliteration:
Agazhvaaraith thaangum nilampoalath thammai,
Igazhvaarp poruththal thalai.
current_meaning: Just as the earth keeps holding up even the people who dig into it, the highest virtue is to patiently bear with those who insult and belittle us.
elementary_explanation: Think about the ground under your feet. People dig holes in it, stomp on it and poke it with shovels, and it still holds everybody up without complaining. This kural says the best kind of person is like that ground: when someone is mean to you, you stay steady and kind instead of hitting back.
university_explanation: Valluvar opens the chapter with one of the most famous images in Tamil ethics: the earth (நிலம்) that supports the very people who dig into it (அகழ்வார்). The two verbs are set side by side on purpose. அகழ் (to dig, to wound the ground) matches இகழ் (to scorn, to wound with words), so an insult is pictured as digging into a person, and the patient person takes it in the way soil does, without caving in. Commentators such as Mu. Varadarasan and Solomon Pappaiah point out that the earth doesn't just put up with the digger; it keeps holding him up so he doesn't fall, which makes endurance an active kind of support. The last word, தலை ('the foremost'), puts forbearance at the head of the virtues and sets up the thesis the rest of the chapter develops. Other traditions reach for the same metaphor: the Sanskrit kṣamā means both 'earth' and 'forgiveness,' and the Buddha compares abusive speech to a man trying to dig away the whole earth with a hoe.

tamil:
பொறுத்தல் இறப்பினை என்றும் அதனை
மறத்தல் அதனினும் நன்று.
transliteration:
Poruththal irappinai endrum adhanai,
Maraththal adhaninum nandru.
current_meaning: Always bear with wrongs done to you, even ones that go beyond all limits. Forgetting them completely is better still.
elementary_explanation: If a friend breaks your favorite toy, being patient about it is good. This kural says something is even better: letting it go so completely that you stop thinking about it. Holding onto a hurt is like carrying a heavy rock in your pocket, and forgetting it is like finally throwing the rock away.
university_explanation: The couplet sets up two steps: பொறுத்தல் (bearing a wrong) and, higher still, மறத்தல் (forgetting it). The key word இறப்பு here means 'transgression, going beyond bounds.' Traditional commentators such as Parimelazhagan and Mu. Varadarasan read it as an excessive wrong, not as 'death,' although some popular modern glosses take it as 'until death.' Valluvar's point is psychological: if you endure a wrong but still keep a record of it, the endurance is incomplete, because the remembered wrong keeps feeding resentment. Real forbearance lets the grievance go altogether. Rabbinic law draws a similar line between taking vengeance and bearing a grudge (Leviticus 19:18, discussed in Talmud Yoma 23a), and Nietzsche later observed that some strong natures 'forgive' simply by forgetting.

tamil:
இன்மையுள் இன்மை விருந்தொரால் வன்மையுள்
வன்மை மடவார்ப் பொறை.
transliteration:
Inmaiyul inmai virundhoraal vanmaiyul,
Vanmai madavaarp porai.
current_meaning: The worst poverty of all is being unable to welcome a guest, and the greatest strength of all is patiently putting up with foolish people.
elementary_explanation: Being poor isn't only about having little money. This kural says the saddest kind of poor is not being able to share even a snack with a friend who visits. Being strong isn't only about big muscles either: the strongest kind of strong is staying calm when someone acts silly or rude to you.
university_explanation: Valluvar builds the couplet on a double superlative, இன்மையுள் இன்மை ('the poverty within poverty') and வன்மையுள் வன்மை ('the strength within strength'), and uses it to pair two virtues that seem unrelated. The first half looks back to the chapter on hospitality (விருந்தோம்பல், ch. 9), where turning away a guest is the gravest failure of a household. The second half redefines might as the ability to bear the provocations of மடவார், 'the ignorant' or 'foolish.' Setting them side by side suggests a shared logic: hospitality and forbearance both measure inner abundance, not outward resources. Redefining strength as self-mastery is one of the most widely shared moral reversals across traditions, from the Mishnah's 'Who is mighty?' to the hadith about the strong man who controls his anger.

tamil:
நிறையுடைமை நீங்காமை வேண்டின் பொறையுடைமை
போற்றி யொழுகப் படும்.
transliteration:
Niraiyudaimai neengaamai vendin poraiyudaimai,
Potri yozhugap padum.
current_meaning: If you never want to lose your fullness of character, your inner completeness and self-possession, you must cherish patience and live by it.
elementary_explanation: Imagine your good character is a glass filled to the top with water. Every time you lose your temper, some spills out. This kural says that if you want to keep your glass full, you have to carry it carefully, which means being patient all the time.
university_explanation: நிறை is a rich Tamil word meaning fullness, completeness, and also self-restraint or integrity. It describes a wife's guarded constancy in chapter 6 and the sages 'full of word' in chapter 3. Valluvar makes பொறையுடைமை (possessing patience) the precondition for keeping நிறையுடைமை (possessing fullness). The two '-உடைமை' compounds deliberately echo each other, which suggests patience is not one virtue among many but the container that keeps the others from leaking away. The phrase போற்றி ஒழுகுதல் ('to guard and live by') implies constant vigilance, not occasional restraint, and Solomon Pappaiah reads நிறை as சான்றாண்மை, the complete nobility of character treated in chapter 99. The Epistle of James makes almost the same claim, that patience is what makes a person 'perfect and entire.'

tamil:
ஒறுத்தாரை ஒன்றாக வையாரே வைப்பர்
பொறுத்தாரைப் பொன்போற் பொதிந்து.
transliteration:
Oruththaarai ondraaga vaiyaare vaippar,
Poruththaaraip ponpor podhindhu.
current_meaning: People count those who punish every wrong done to them as worth nothing. Those who forbear they treasure, keeping them close like wrapped-up gold.
elementary_explanation: Two kids get pushed in the lunch line. One shoves back hard, and the other says, 'It's okay.' Later, which one do people trust and want as a friend? This kural says people treasure the patient one like a piece of gold kept safe in a box, while the one who always hits back isn't valued at all.
university_explanation: ஒறுத்தார் ('those who punished' the offender) and பொறுத்தார் ('those who bore it') differ by a single initial consonant, and Valluvar uses the near-rhyme to make the moral contrast audible. ஒன்றாக வையார் means such people are not counted as anything at all, while பொன்போற் பொதிந்து வைப்பர் ('they wrap and keep like gold') suggests a treasure bundled up and stored with care. The judgement is a social one: honor goes not to the person who wins the exchange of blows but to the one who refuses it. That reverses a warrior-culture instinct that leaving a slight unavenged is shameful. Aristotle is a useful contrast: he praises the good-tempered man who 'tends to make allowances,' but warns that putting up with every insult can look 'slavish.' Valluvar settles that tension firmly on the side of forbearance.

tamil:
ஒறுத்தார்க்கு ஒருநாளை இன்பம் பொறுத்தார்க்குப்
பொன்றுந் துணையும் புகழ்.
transliteration:
Oruththaarkku orunaalai inbam poruththaarkkup,
Pondrun thunaiyum pugazh.
current_meaning: People who take revenge enjoy a pleasure that lasts a single day. People who forbear win a fame that lasts until the world itself passes away.
elementary_explanation: Getting back at someone can feel good, for about one day. Then the good feeling is gone. Being the person who stayed kind is different: people remember it and talk about it for a very, very long time.
university_explanation: The couplet sets two time-scales against each other: ஒருநாளை இன்பம் ('one day's pleasure') and பொன்றுந் துணையும் புகழ் ('fame until [the world] perishes'). Mu. Varadarasan and Solomon Pappaiah read பொன்றும் as the ending of the world, while Kalaignar reads it as 'throughout one's life.' Either way the basic contrast between passing gratification and lasting reputation holds. Valluvar is speaking the language of புகழ், the enduring renown he devotes chapter 24 to, where reputation is treated as the only thing that outlives the body. The psychological point is sharp: Aristotle also observes that revenge 'relieves' anger by 'producing ... pleasure instead of pain,' but Valluvar insists that this pleasure is the shortest-lived of goods.

tamil:
திறனல்ல தற்பிறர் செய்யினும் நோநொந்து
அறனல்ல செய்யாமை நன்று.
transliteration:
Thiranalla tharpirar seyyinum nononthu,
Aranalla seyyaamai nandru.
current_meaning: Even when others do you harm you never deserved, it is good to feel sorry for the suffering their wrongdoing will bring on them, and not to do anything unrighteous in return.
elementary_explanation: When someone is unfair to you, you might want to be unfair back. This kural says don't. Instead, feel a little sad for them, because doing wrong usually comes back to hurt the person who does it, and keep doing the right thing yourself.
university_explanation: The key phrase is நோநொந்து. Mu. Varadarasan reads it as grieving over the suffering (நோ) that will fall on the wrongdoer as the fruit of his act, which makes the couplet an ethic of compassion toward the offender rather than mere self-restraint. Solomon Pappaiah offers a slightly different nuance, grieving at the thought that retaliation would hurt him, but both readings end in refusing அறனல்ல, 'what is not dharma.' The couplet therefore goes beyond tolerance to a positive moral stance: being injured doesn't license you to abandon virtue. Socrates states the same principle in the Crito, that it is never right to return wrong for wrong, and Jesus acts it out on the cross by praying for those who crucify him.

tamil:
மிகுதியான் மிக்கவை செய்தாரைத் தாந்தம்
தகுதியான் வென்று விடல்.
transliteration:
Migudhiyaan mikkavai seydhaaraith thaandham,
Thagudhiyaan vendru vidal.
current_meaning: When people swollen with arrogance heap outrageous wrongs on you, defeat them through your own worth, that is, through your patience.
elementary_explanation: Sometimes a bully acts big and mean, and you might think the only way to win is to be even meaner. This kural says you can beat them another way: by staying calm and good. Your patience works like a superpower that makes their meanness look small.
university_explanation: The couplet plays on மிகுதி ('excess, arrogance') and தகுதி ('fitness, worth'). The aggressor acts out of surplus (மிகுதியான் மிக்கவை, 'excessive deeds out of excess'), and is to be overcome by the victim's own proper measure (தாந்தம் தகுதியான்). Commentators consistently identify this தகுதி with பொறை, patience itself, so forbearance becomes a strategy for victory rather than passive defeat. The verb, வென்று விடல் ('conquer'), is deliberately martial: Valluvar claims the vocabulary of winning for the person who doesn't retaliate. The same logic appears in Paul's 'overcome evil with good,' in the Qur'an's 'repel evil with what is better,' and in Vidura's maxim that anger is conquered by forgiveness, a maxim that reappears almost word for word in the Dhammapada (v. 223).

tamil:
துறந்தாரின் தூய்மை உடையர் இறந்தார்வாய்
இன்னாச்சொல் நோற்கிற் பவர்.
transliteration:
Thurandhaarin thooimai udaiyar irandhaarvaai,
Innaachchol norkir pavar.
current_meaning: Those who can patiently bear the harsh words of people who overstep every limit are as pure as those who have renounced the world.
elementary_explanation: Monks and nuns who give up everything are often thought of as very pure. This kural says you don't have to leave home to be that pure. If someone yells nasty words at you and you stay calm, your heart is just as clean as theirs.
university_explanation: இறந்தார் here doesn't mean 'the dead.' It means 'those who have transgressed' (from இற, to go beyond), the same root as இறப்பு in Kural 152. Mu. Varadarasan and Kalaignar confirm this sense, though some popular glosses take it literally. The comparison with துறந்தார் ('renunciants') matters because these chapters belong to இல்லறவியல், the section on the householder's life: Valluvar claims that a householder who endures insult reaches the purity normally reserved for ascetics. Solomon Pappaiah makes this explicit, saying that even living a household life, such a person is as pure as a renunciant. The verb நோற்றல் ('to endure as an austerity') anticipates the next couplet's comparison with fasting and recasts patience itself as a form of tapas.

tamil:
உண்ணாது நோற்பார் பெரியர் பிறர்சொல்லும்
இன்னாச்சொல் நோற்பாரின் பின்.
transliteration:
Unnaadhu norpaar periyar pirarsollum,
Innaachchol norpaarin pin.
current_meaning: Those who fast and endure hunger are great, but they rank only after those who endure the cruel words other people speak to them.
elementary_explanation: Going without food for a whole day to be good is really hard, and people admire it. This kural says something is even harder and better: when someone says mean things to you and you swallow your anger and stay kind, you are the real champion.
university_explanation: Valluvar closes the chapter by ranking two kinds of நோன்பு (austerity): உண்ணாது நோற்றல், enduring hunger by fasting, and இன்னாச்சொல் நோற்றல், enduring cruel speech. By placing the faster 'after' (பின்) the one who bears insult, he puts the most visible ascetic practice of his time, prominent in both Jain and Brahmanical asceticism, below an inner, social virtue. Repeating நோற்பார் in both lines insists that patience is itself tapas, completing the argument begun in Kural 159. The ranking resonates with the Dhammapada's 'Enduring patience is the highest austerity,' with the hadith that tells a fasting person to answer abuse by saying 'I am fasting,' and with Isaiah's prophetic critique that a true fast is measured by ethical conduct.

tamil:
ஒழுக்காறாக் கொள்க ஒருவன்தன் நெஞ்சத்து
அழுக்காறு இலாத இயல்பு.
transliteration:
Ozhukkaaraak kolga oruvanthan nenjathu
Azhukkaaru ilaadha iyalbu.
current_meaning: Let a person adopt, as the very rule of their conduct, a nature whose heart holds no envy.
elementary_explanation: Some families have house rules, like “always say please.” This kural says: make “never be jealous of anyone” one of your own rules, as important as any other rule for being good.
university_explanation: Valluvar builds the chapter on a pun: ஒழுக்காறு (ozhukkaaru, “the path of right conduct”) and அழுக்காறு (azhukkaaru, “the path of impurity,” i.e., envy) differ by a single sound, so the couplet sets the right road against the soiled road. He places the absence of envy inside the heart (நெஞ்சத்து), not just in outward behavior, which treats envy as a flaw of character rather than a wrong act. Commentators from Parimelazhagar to Mu. Varadarasanar read the couplet as saying freedom from envy should be held as seriously as the formal rules of ozhukkam (Chapter 14). The view is close to Aristotle's, who counted envy among the passions whose very names imply badness, and to the Buddhist idea that a disposition must be trained, not merely a deed avoided.

tamil:
விழுப்பேற்றின் அஃதொப்பது இல்லையார் மாட்டும்
அழுக்காற்றின் அன்மை பெறின்.
transliteration:
Vizhuppetrin aqdhoppadhu illaiyaar maattum
Azhukkaatrin anmai perin.
current_meaning: If a person can be free of envy toward everyone, no other excellent gain they could ever obtain is equal to it.
elementary_explanation: Imagine a treasure chest full of prizes: gold, trophies, toys. This kural says the best prize is a heart that is never jealous of anyone. Better than all the rest.
university_explanation: The key phrase is யார் மாட்டும் (“toward anyone at all”): Valluvar asks for complete freedom from envy, not selective freedom. Envy usually targets equals, as Aristotle observed, so envying no one means refusing to compare one's own standing with others'. By calling this the highest of all விழுப்பேறு (excellent attainments), the couplet puts an inner state above wealth, fame, and learning. The point anticipates the Stoic claim that goods in our control are the only true goods, and that once we see this, “there will be no room for envy.”

tamil:
அறன்ஆக்கம் வேண்டாதான் என்பான் பிறனாக்கம்
பேணாது அழுக்கறுப் பான்.
transliteration:
Aran aakkam vendaadhaan enbaan piranaakkam
Penaadhu azhukkaruppaan.
current_meaning: A person who, instead of welcoming another's prosperity, envies it, is effectively someone who wants neither virtue nor prosperity for themselves.
elementary_explanation: If your friend wins a prize and you sulk instead of cheering, you're not just being unkind to them. You're blocking your own chance to be good and to do well. Being jealous is like saying “I don't want good things for myself either.”
university_explanation: The couplet makes a psychological claim: envy is self-defeating, not just unkind. Parimelazhagar reads அறனாக்கம் as both அறம் (virtue) and ஆக்கம் (prosperity). The envious person's attitude implicitly rejects both, since virtue grows through goodwill and prosperity through good conduct. பேணாது (“without cherishing”) implies the right response to another's good fortune is active appreciation, close to the Buddhist mudita (sympathetic joy). Aristotle's definition fits closely: the envious man “is pained at all good fortune,” even when it is deserved.

tamil:
அழுக்காற்றின் அல்லவை செய்யார் இழுக்காற்றின்
ஏதம் படுபாக்கு அறிந்து.
transliteration:
Azhukkaatrin allavai seyyaar izhukkaatrin
Edham padupaakku arindhu.
current_meaning: The wise, knowing the suffering that comes from walking a wrong path, will not do wrong because of envy.
elementary_explanation: If you know a path has a big muddy pit, you don't walk that way. Wise people know jealousy leads to doing mean things, and mean things lead to trouble, so they don't let jealousy push them into it.
university_explanation: The subject, “the wise” (அறிவுடையோர்), is understood from context, as the commentators note. The couplet treats restraint from envy-driven wrongdoing as a matter of knowledge: seeing where the “fault-path” (இழுக்காறு) leads. Valluvar moves from the feeling of envy (azhukkaaru) to the acts it produces (அல்லவை, unrighteous deeds), and the wise stop the chain at the first link. The reasoning is prudential as well as moral, like the Buddha's image of the trader who avoids a dangerous road. It also matches Aristotle's claim that envy, like theft or murder, has no right amount or right occasion; it is always a mistake.

tamil:
அழுக்காறு உடையார்க்கு அதுசாலும் ஒன்னார்
வழுக்காயும் கேடீன் பது.
transliteration:
Azhukkaaru udaiyaarkku adhusaalum onnaar
Vazhukkaayum kedeenbadhu.
current_meaning: For the envious, envy alone is enough. Even if their enemies fail to harm them, envy itself will bring about their ruin.
elementary_explanation: Imagine someone who never needs a bully to hurt them, because they keep hurting themselves by feeling jealous all the time. Envy is like a bully that lives inside you.
university_explanation: The phrase அது சாலும் (“that is enough”) makes envy a self-sufficient engine of destruction. No external enemy (ஒன்னார்) is needed, and even if enemies falter (வழுக்காயும்), envy does not. The same insight appears across traditions: Proverbs calls envy “the rottenness of the bones,” Ovid pictures Envy gnawing herself, and the Dhammapada compares the depraved man to a creeper that strangles its own host tree. Aristotle's definition explains why: envy is pain at another's good that brings the envier no gain, only suffering.

tamil:
கொடுப்பது அழுக்கறுப்பான் சுற்றம் உடுப்பதூஉம்
உண்பதூஉம் இன்றிக் கெடும்.
transliteration:
Koduppadhu azhukkaruppaan sutram uduppadhoovum
Unbadhoovum indrik kedum.
current_meaning: One who is envious of what is given to others will perish, along with his kin, without even clothing to wear or food to eat.
elementary_explanation: Imagine a kid who gets upset every time a teacher gives stickers to others. Eventually, nobody wants to share with that kid or their friends either. Being jealous of other people's gifts leaves you, and the people around you, with nothing.
university_explanation: This couplet narrows envy to a specific form: resentment of generosity itself (கொடுப்பது, “what is given”), whether one objects to a gift going to someone else or tries to stop it. The punishment is social and material: not only the envier but his சுற்றம் (kin, dependents) are left without food or clothing, since the grudging spirit cuts the household off from the web of mutual giving. The idea has a close counterpart in the Buddha's teaching that whoever obstructs another's gift harms three parties, beginning with himself. Pirkei Avot likewise names the giver who wishes others would not give as having an “evil eye” toward what belongs to others.

tamil:
அவ்வித்து அழுக்காறு உடையானைச் செய்யவள்
தவ்வையைக் காட்டி விடும்.
transliteration:
Avvithu azhukkaaru udaiyaanaich cheyyaval
Thavvaiyaik kaatti vidum.
current_meaning: The goddess of fortune (Lakshmi, “the red one”), resenting the envious man, leaves him and points him out to her elder sister, the goddess of misfortune.
elementary_explanation: Imagine Good Luck as a friendly person who visits your house. When she sees you're always jealous, she leaves, and on her way out she tells her grumpy sister, Bad Luck, “This house is yours now.”
university_explanation: Valluvar here uses a mythological image unusual for a text that mostly avoids sectarian deities. செய்யவள் (“the red/fair one”) is Lakshmi (Tiru), and தவ்வை (“elder sister”) is Mudevi/Jyeshtha, goddess of misfortune, who in the Padma and Linga Puranas rises from the churned ocean before Lakshmi and is told to dwell among the quarrelsome and wicked. அவ்வித்து is read by Parimelazhagar as “being herself envious [of him],” so the goddess answers envy with envy, a measure-for-measure punishment. The image turns an abstract claim, that envy drives away prosperity, into a vivid scene, a technique Valluvar uses sparingly and to strong effect.

tamil:
அழுக்காறு எனஒரு பாவி திருச்செற்றுத்
தீயுழி உய்த்து விடும்.
transliteration:
Azhukkaaru ena oru paavi thiruchchetruth
Theeyuzhi uyththu vidum.
current_meaning: Envy, a sinner without equal, destroys a person's wealth and drives him onto the path of evil, even into the fire of hell.
elementary_explanation: Envy is like a sneaky thief who first steals everything you have, then pushes you onto a dangerous road. Once envy moves in, it takes your good things away and leads you somewhere bad.
university_explanation: Valluvar personifies envy as a பாவி (sinner, evil being) with no equal (ஒரு), and gives it two acts: it destroys wealth (திருச்செற்று, with திரு again evoking Lakshmi from the previous couplet) and drives its host into தீயுழி. The term means “evil place” or “evil path”; Parimelazhagar and Solomon Pappaiah read it as hell, others as a life of wrongdoing. The double sense covers both this-worldly ruin and afterlife punishment, a pattern also seen in the Dhammapada's “suffers here and hereafter.” Parallels such as Korah and Devadatta, whose envy ended with the earth swallowing them, show how widely traditions have linked envy to a downward plunge.

tamil:
அவ்விய நெஞ்சத்தான் ஆக்கமும் செவ்வியான்
கேடும் நினைக்கப் படும்.
transliteration:
Avviya nenjathaan aakkamum sevviyaan
Kedum ninaikkap padum.
current_meaning: The prosperity of a person with an envious heart, and the misfortune of an upright one, are things that must be pondered, for they are anomalies that call for explanation.
elementary_explanation: Sometimes a mean, jealous kid seems to get everything, while a kind kid has a hard time. That looks unfair, and this kural says: stop and think about it. Things may not stay that way, and there is a deeper reason behind it.
university_explanation: Valluvar recognizes the classic problem of theodicy: the wicked sometimes prosper and the good sometimes suffer. He does not deny it. He calls these cases நினைக்கப்படும், “to be reflected upon.” Parimelazhagar resolves the anomaly through karma: the envious man's prosperity comes from past merit now being used up, and the good man's suffering from past deeds now being paid off, so neither lasts. The same wrestling appears in Psalm 73, in Rabbi Yannai's admission in Pirkei Avot, in the Dhammapada's teaching that evil “ripens” late, and in Glaucon's challenge in Plato's Republic, which makes this one of the most widely shared questions in world ethics.

tamil:
அழுக்கற்று அகன்றாரும் இல்லை அஃதுஇல்லார்
பெருக்கத்தில் தீர்ந்தாரும் இல்.
transliteration:
Azhukkatru akandraarum illai aqdhuillaar
Perukkaththil theerndhaarum il.
current_meaning: No one has ever risen to greatness through envy, and no one free from envy has ever fallen away from prosperity.
elementary_explanation: Being jealous has never helped anyone become great, not even once. And people who are happy for others never end up losing out because of it. So jealousy has zero upside, and kindness has zero downside.
university_explanation: The chapter closes with a balanced pair of universal negatives: அழுக்கற்று அகன்றாரும் இல்லை (none have grown great through envy; அகன்றார், literally “expanded”) and அஃதில்லார் பெருக்கத்தில் தீர்ந்தாரும் இல் (none without it have been cut off from increase). The form is a complete disjunction: envy never helps and its absence never hurts, so envy is irrational even on purely selfish grounds. Read with Kural 169, the couplet resolves the anomaly: apparent exceptions are temporary and the long-run pattern holds. The prudential argument matches Epictetus: if someone gains an advantage by paying a price you did not pay, “don't imagine that he has gained any advantage over you.”

tamil:
நடுவின்றி நன்பொருள் வெஃகின் குடிபொன்றிக்
குற்றமும் ஆங்கே தரும்.
transliteration:
Naduvindri nanporul vehkin kudiponrik
Kutramum aange tharum.
current_meaning: If a person abandons fairness and sets his heart on the good property that belongs to someone else, that very desire will bring ruin on his family and guilt on himself, right then and there.
elementary_explanation: Imagine wanting your classmate’s new bike so badly that you stop caring what is fair. This kural says that kind of wanting is like a crack in your own house: it doesn’t just get you in trouble, it hurts your whole family too.
university_explanation: The chapter opens with its thesis in its strongest form: covetousness (வெஃகுதல், vehkuthal) is condemned not only as an act of seizure but as a desire born of abandoning நடு (nadu), the equity or impartiality Valluvar had already exalted in chapter 12 (நடுவு நிலைமை). The consequences are twofold and immediate: the family line (குடி, kudi) is destroyed and guilt (குற்றம்) accrues, and the word ஆங்கே (aange, “right there, at that moment”) insists that the damage is not deferred to a future birth but arrives simultaneously with the desire. Parimelazhagar reads the kural as addressed to the householder, which explains why the penalty falls on the kudi: the covetous man betrays the very household he is supposed to sustain. The idea that injustice in acquisition corrodes the acquirer’s own house recurs across traditions, from the Hebrew story of Achan to Aristotle’s analysis of pleonexia as a vice of unfairness (anisotes).

tamil:
படுபயன் வெஃகிப் பழிப்படுவ செய்யார்
நடுவன்மை நாணு பவர்.
transliteration:
Padupayan vehkip pazhippaduva seyyaar
Naduvanmai naanu pavar.
current_meaning: People who feel shame at the very idea of being unfair will never do disgraceful things just because they want the profit they could get from them.
elementary_explanation: Suppose you could win a game by quietly peeking at someone’s cards. A person who would feel embarrassed to cheat just won’t do it, even if it means winning. This kural says that feeling of shame protects you from doing wrong for a prize.
university_explanation: Where kural 171 threatened consequences, 172 names the internal safeguard: நாண் (naan), a moral sense of shame or modesty, here specifically shame at நடுவன்மை (naduvanmai, “non-equity”). The phrase படுபயன் (padupayan) denotes the gain that “falls” to one, the benefit that would accrue from taking another’s property, and பழிப்படுவ (pazhippaduva) are acts that incur public blame. Valluvar’s psychology is notable: the person of integrity is restrained less by fear of punishment than by an internalised aversion to injustice, a theme developed fully in chapter 102 (நாணுடைமை). This aligns with Gita ethics, in which modesty (Sanskrit hri) and the reflex of weighing gain against righteousness are marks of a mature moral agent.

tamil:
சிற்றின்பம் வெஃகி அறனல்ல செய்யாரே
மற்றின்பம் வேண்டு பவர்.
transliteration:
Sitrinbam vehki aranalla seyyaare
Matrinbam vendu pavar.
current_meaning: Those who seek the other, lasting joy will never do unrighteous things just to grab a small, passing pleasure.
elementary_explanation: If you are saving your pocket money for something you really love, you won’t spend it on a cheap sweet that’s gone in a minute. This kural says people who want the big, lasting kind of happiness don’t do bad things for tiny, quick treats.
university_explanation: The kural sets up a contrast between சிற்றின்பம் (sitrinbam, “petty pleasure”) and மற்றின்பம் (matrinbam, “the other joy”). Parimelazhagar glosses the latter as the bliss of heaven or liberation, while modern commentators such as Mu. Varadarasan read it as the enduring happiness that flows from aram (virtue); either way, the argument is a rational trade-off, not a prohibition. Covetousness is foolish because it sacrifices a greater, lasting good for a trivial, fleeting one. This is among the most widely shared structures in world ethics: the Buddha’s ‘renounce the lesser happiness for the greater’, Nachiketas refusing Death’s riches, and Socrates rebuking Athens for preferring money to the soul all have the same shape.

tamil:
இலமென்று வெஃகுதல் செய்யார் புலம்வென்ற
புன்மையில் காட்சி யவர்.
transliteration:
Ilamendru vehkuthal seyyaar pulamvendra
Punmaiyil kaatchi yavar.
current_meaning: People of flawless insight who have mastered their senses will not covet what belongs to others, not even when they think, “We are poor and have nothing.”
elementary_explanation: It is easy not to want your friend’s lunch when you already have a big one. This kural is about someone who is really hungry and still doesn’t take what isn’t theirs, because they’ve trained themselves to be strong inside.
university_explanation: This kural removes the most sympathetic excuse for covetousness: need. இலம் என்று (ilam endru, “saying ‘we have nothing’”) captures the self-justifying thought of the poor, and Valluvar insists that even this does not license desire for another’s goods among those who are புலம் வென்ற (pulam venra, “sense-conquered”) and of புன்மையில் காட்சி (punmaiyil kaatchi, “vision free from meanness”). The pairing of sense-mastery with non-covetousness is characteristically Indian (compare the Gita’s sthitaprajna), but the insistence that integrity must survive poverty is universal, as Agur’s prayer in Proverbs attests. Valluvar is not romanticising poverty; he is arguing that virtue that fails under pressure was never virtue.

tamil:
அஃகி அகன்ற அறிவென்னாம் யார்மாட்டும்
வெஃகி வெறிய செயின்.
transliteration:
Ahki akandra arivennaam yaarmaattum
Vehki veriya seyin.
current_meaning: What good is a mind that is both sharp and broad, if its owner covets other people’s things and behaves senselessly toward anyone at all?
elementary_explanation: Imagine the smartest kid in class who uses their brains to trick friends out of their toys. Being clever doesn’t make that okay; it just makes the cleverness useless. This kural says being smart means nothing if greed makes you act foolishly.
university_explanation: The first line is a small masterpiece of sound and sense: அஃகி அகன்ற அறிவு (ahki akandra arivu) describes knowledge that is at once narrowed to a fine point (ahku, ‘to become subtle/minute’) and broadened (akal, ‘to spread wide’), in other words both deep and wide. The rhetorical question ‘என்னாம்?’ (ennaam, ‘of what use?’) then cancels that learning entirely if its possessor, driven by covetousness, does வெறிய (veriya, senseless or improper deeds) toward யார்மாட்டும் (yaarmaattum, ‘anyone whatsoever’). The kural anticipates the chapter on learning (40-43) by insisting that intellect is not a moral safeguard; covetousness can hijack it. The Gita’s chain of desire, anger, delusion, and ‘loss of intelligence’ and Plato’s image of reason enslaved to money-making make the same diagnosis.

tamil:
அருள்வெஃகி ஆற்றின்கண் நின்றான் பொருள்வெஃகிப்
பொல்லாத சூழக் கெடும்.
transliteration:
Arulvehki aatrinkan nindraan porulvehkip
Pollaadha soozhak kedum.
current_meaning: Even a person who has longed for grace and stood firmly on the path of virtue will be ruined if he starts coveting others’ wealth and plotting wicked ways to get it.
elementary_explanation: Think of a kid who has always been kind and helpful. If one day they start scheming to take someone else’s things, all that goodness can come crashing down. This kural says no one is so good that greed can’t ruin them.
university_explanation: The kural turns on a deliberate repetition: the same verb வெஃகு (vehku, ‘to desire’) is used for the noble desire for அருள் (arul, grace/compassion) and the base desire for பொருள் (porul, wealth). The same faculty of longing can be aimed upward or downward, and a person who has aimed it well can still redirect it disastrously. ஆற்றின்கண் நின்றான் (aatrinkan nindraan, ‘one who stood in the path’) is read by Parimelazhagar as the householder’s path by which grace is attained, and more broadly by modern commentators as the path of virtue; பொல்லாத சூழ (pollaadha soozha) stresses that plotting is itself ruinous, even before any theft. The kural is a warning against spiritual complacency, echoed in the Gita’s admission that the senses carry away even a striving sage, and in the Qur’anic portrait of the man raised by signs who ‘adhered to the earth’.

tamil:
வேண்டற்க வெஃகியாம் ஆக்கம் விளைவயின்
மாண்டற் கரிதாம் பயன்.
transliteration:
Vendarka vehkiyaam aakkam vilaivayin
Maandar karithaam payan.
current_meaning: Do not wish for prosperity that comes from coveting others’ goods; when it finally ripens, its fruit will rarely turn out to be good.
elementary_explanation: It’s like planting a seed you stole from your neighbour’s garden. It might grow, but the fruit tastes bitter because you know how you got it. This kural says wealth you got by grabbing others’ things never gives you a truly good harvest.
university_explanation: The kural uses an agricultural metaphor: வெஃகியாம் ஆக்கம் (vehkiyaam aakkam, ‘increase that comes through coveting’) is a crop, and விளைவயின் (vilaivayin, ‘at the time of its ripening’) its fruit is மாண்டற்கு அரிது (maandarku arithu, ‘hard to be excellent’). The argument concerns delayed consequences: ill-gotten gain may look like prosperity at first, but its maturation reveals its true nature. Some commentators (e.g., Solomon Pappaiah) read maandal as ‘goodness’ in enjoyment, while others read it as ‘glory’; either way the gain proves hollow. The theme of sweet-at-first, bitter-at-the-end fruit links this kural to the Gita’s account of rajasic happiness and to Proverbs’ ‘bread of deceit.’

tamil:
அஃகாமை செல்வத்திற்கு யாதெனின் வெஃகாமை
வேண்டும் பிறன்கைப் பொருள்.
transliteration:
Ahkaamai selvaththirku yaadhenin vehkaamai
Vendum pirankaip porul.
current_meaning: If you ask what keeps one’s wealth from dwindling, the answer is this: do not covet the property in another person’s hands.
elementary_explanation: If you want to keep your own toys safe, the best rule is never to grab other people’s toys. Then no one has a reason to take yours, and you stay happy with what you have. This kural says not wanting other people’s things is the secret to keeping your own.
university_explanation: The kural is built on a pun that is lost in translation: அஃகாமை (ahkaamai, ‘non-diminishing’) and வெஃகாமை (vehkaamai, ‘non-coveting’) differ by a single consonant, so the grammar of the line enacts its claim that the one secures the other. It is framed as a riddle with its own answer (‘yaadhenin…’, ‘if one asks what…’), a didactic device Valluvar uses often. பிறன் கைப் பொருள் (piran kaip porul, ‘property in another’s hand’) pointedly includes even possessions casually within reach. The ethical logic is both moral and practical: a society in which people do not covet is one in which everyone’s wealth is secure, and a mind that does not covet does not feel its own wealth as insufficient. The kural thus unites the tenth commandment’s social function with the Upanishadic ‘do not covet’ as a spiritual discipline.

tamil:
அறனறிந்து வெஃகா அறிவுடையார்ச் சேரும்
திறன்அறிந் தாங்கே திரு.
transliteration:
Aranarindhu vehkaa arivudaiyaarch serum
Thiranarin thaange thiru.
current_meaning: Fortune, the goddess Thiru, recognises the worth of the wise who understand virtue and do not covet others’ goods, and she comes to them on her own accord, finding her way to them.
elementary_explanation: Imagine good luck as a friend who likes visiting kind, honest people. This kural says if you know what’s right and don’t try to take other people’s things, good fortune will find its way to your door by itself.
university_explanation: திரு (thiru), glossed by all traditional commentators as Lakshmi (Thirumagal), the goddess of fortune, is here personified as an agent with judgment: திறன் அறிந்து (thiran arindhu) means she ‘knows the proper way’ or ‘recognises their merit’ and arrives ஆங்கே (aange, ‘right there’). The kural thus reverses the covetous logic: the coveter reaches for wealth and loses it, while the one who does not reach is sought out by wealth itself. Parimelazhagar’s gloss emphasises that these people are அறிவுடையார் (arivudaiyaar) who know aram, so their restraint is a considered moral choice, not mere passivity. The idea that virtue attracts prosperity has close analogues in the Gita’s closing verse (where ‘sri’ accompanies righteousness), Socrates’ ‘from virtue come money and every other good’, and the Buddhist teaching that the righteous non-coveter may reappear among those of ‘great property’.

tamil:
இறலீனும் எண்ணாது வெஃகின் விறல்ஈனும்
வேண்டாமை என்னுஞ் செருக்கு.
transliteration:
Iraleenum ennaadhu vehkin viraleenum
Vendaamai ennum serukku.
current_meaning: Coveting others’ property without thinking of the consequences gives birth to destruction; the proud strength of simply not wanting gives birth to victory.
elementary_explanation: Grabbing for something that isn’t yours without thinking is like reaching into a fire: you get burned. But being strong enough to say “I don’t need that” is like winning a race. This kural says not wanting is a kind of superpower.
university_explanation: The chapter closes with a perfectly balanced antithesis built on a rhyme: இறல் ஈனும் (iral eenum, ‘gives birth to destruction’) against விறல் ஈனும் (viral eenum, ‘gives birth to victory’). The verb ஈன் (een, ‘to bear, as offspring’) makes both outcomes the natural children of their causes. எண்ணாது (ennaadhu, ‘without reflecting’) identifies thoughtlessness about consequences as the root of covetousness, while வேண்டாமை என்னும் செருக்கு (vendaamai ennum serukku) calls non-desire a kind of செருக்கு (serukku, ‘pride, exaltation, greatness’). Valluvar reclaims a word usually negative and makes it the dignity of the person who needs nothing from others. The idea that restraint is itself a victory appears in Epictetus, in the Qur’anic promise of success to those saved from their own avarice, and in the Buddhist ‘craving-freed’ who vanquishes all suffering.

tamil:
அறங்கூறான் அல்ல செயினும் ஒருவன்
புறங்கூறான் என்றல் இனிது.
transliteration:
Arangooraan alla seyinum oruvan,
Purangooraan endral inidhu.
current_meaning: Even if a man never speaks a word in praise of virtue and does nothing but wrong, it is still something good if people can say of him, “At least he does not speak ill of others behind their backs.”
elementary_explanation: Imagine a kid who forgets his homework, is messy, and gets into trouble a lot. But everyone says, “He never talks badly about anyone when they’re not around.” That one good thing still shines. This kural says not gossiping about people behind their backs is so important that even someone with lots of faults earns a little praise for it.
university_explanation: Valluvar opens the chapter with a deliberately provocative concession: he imagines a man who neither professes aram (virtue) nor practises it, and still finds one thing worth saying in his favour — that he is not a backbiter (puṟaṅkūṟāṉ, literally “one who speaks at the back”). The rhetorical move establishes a hierarchy of vices before any argument is made: slander is placed so low that merely abstaining from it counts as a redeeming trait. The verb “enṟal” (“that it be said”) is significant; the good in question is reputational, located in what the community can truthfully say of the man, which neatly mirrors the fact that backbiting is itself a crime against another’s reputation. Commentators such as Parimelazhagar read the couplet as an argument a fortiori: if non-slander redeems even the unrighteous, how much more is it required of the righteous. The chapter sits in the householder section (Illaraviyal) right after Envy and Covetousness, reflecting a sequence from inner vices to their expression in speech.

tamil:
அறனழீஇ அல்லவை செய்தலின் தீதே
புறனழீஇப் பொய்த்து நகை.
transliteration:
Aranazheei allavai seydhalin theedhe,
Puranazheeip poiththu nagai.
current_meaning: To tear a person down behind his back and then smile falsely at him to his face is worse than openly rejecting virtue and doing evil.
elementary_explanation: Suppose a classmate says mean things about you when you’re gone, then comes up and grins at you like your best friend. That’s worse than someone who is just openly naughty — because the fake smile is a trick. This kural says the two-faced person is worse than the openly bad one.
university_explanation: The couplet is built on a pointed parallelism: aṟaṉ-aḻīi (“destroying virtue”) against puṟaṉ-aḻīi (“destroying [someone] at the back”), with the second judged worse (tītē). What tips the scale is the final phrase poyttu nakai, “smiling falsely” — the backbiter compounds slander with a feigned intimacy in the victim’s presence. Valluvar is thus condemning not only malicious speech but hypocrisy as a structure of relationship, a split between the face and the back that corrupts the trust on which the householder’s social world rests. The claim that this is worse than open wickedness anticipates a widely shared intuition across ethical traditions: the open enemy can be guarded against, but the smiling detractor disarms his victim first. The verse also sharpens 181: there, abstaining from slander redeemed a sinner; here, slander joined to false friendliness sinks a man below the sinner.

tamil:
புறங்கூறிப் பொய்த்துயிர் வாழ்தலின் சாதல்
அறங்கூற்றும் ஆக்கத் தரும்.
transliteration:
Purangoorip poiththuyir vaazhdhalin saadhal,
Arangootrum aakkath tharum.
current_meaning: Rather than staying alive by backbiting people and being false to their faces, it is better to die; death brings the true gain that the teachings of virtue speak of.
elementary_explanation: Imagine you could stay popular only by telling mean secrets about your friends and pretending to be nice to them. This kural says it’s better to lose everything than to live that way — being a good, honest person matters more than anything you could win by gossip.
university_explanation: The couplet raises the stakes from comparison of vices to a comparison between a way of life and death itself. Puṟaṅkūṟip poyttu uyir vāḻtal — “living by backbiting and falsehood” — names a whole livelihood, the courtier’s or social climber’s art of advancing by undermining others. Against this Valluvar sets cātal, death, which paradoxically yields ākkam (prosperity, gain) of the kind that aṟam-kūṟṟu, the pronouncements of the moral treatises, recognise. Parimelazhagar and Mu. Varadarasan gloss the death as dying in poverty for having refused such conduct — a reading that turns the verse into a choice between material survival bought by slander and moral gain secured by refusing it. The structure echoes a theme found across classical ethics: that there are lives not worth living, and that moral ruin is a worse fate than death.

tamil:
கண்ணின்று கண்ணறச் சொல்லினும் சொல்லற்க
முன்னின்று பின்நோக்காச் சொல்.
transliteration:
Kannindru kannarach chollinum sollarka,
Munnindru pinnokkaach chol.
current_meaning: You may even speak harshly and without kindness to a person’s face, but never speak words behind his back without thinking about the harm they will cause.
elementary_explanation: If your friend does something wrong, it’s okay to tell them straight to their face, even if it’s hard to hear. What’s not okay is saying it to others when your friend isn’t there. Say it to their face or don’t say it at all.
university_explanation: The couplet turns on a set of spatial and visual puns. Kaṇ niṉṟu (“standing before the eyes”) is paired with kaṇ aṟa (“with the eye cut off,” i.e., without kaṇṇōṭṭam, the courteous regard that Valluvar treats as a virtue in chapter 58), while muṉ niṉṟu (“having stood in front”) contrasts with piṉ nōkkā col, which carries two senses: words that do not look to consequences, and words aimed at someone’s back. Valluvar concedes a real cost — harsh, face-to-face speech is not ideal — but ranks it clearly above secret disparagement, because direct speech leaves the target free to answer, correct, or defend himself. This makes the verse a procedural ethic of speech: criticism is legitimate in principle, but its moral character depends on the presence of the person criticised. The same structure appears in legal ideals of hearing both parties and in religious norms of private, direct rebuke.

tamil:
அறஞ்சொல்லும் நெஞ்சத்தான் அன்மை புறஞ்சொல்லும்
புன்மையாற் காணப் படும்.
transliteration:
Aranjollum nenjaththaan anmai puranjollum,
Punmaiyaal kaanap padum.
current_meaning: However much a man talks about virtue, the pettiness of his backbiting shows that his heart is not truly given to virtue.
elementary_explanation: Someone might always say, “Be kind! Be fair!” But if you hear them gossiping meanly about people when those people leave, you know they don’t really mean what they say. Gossip is like a window that lets you see what’s really inside a person.
university_explanation: Here Valluvar turns backbiting into evidence. The phrase aṟañ-collum neñcattāṉ — one whose heart speaks of virtue, or, as many commentators read it, one who merely talks virtue — sets up a contrast between profession and inner reality, and puṟañ-collum puṉmai (“the meanness of speaking at the back”) becomes the diagnostic sign that exposes the gap. The verse therefore makes slander not only a wrong but a symptom: a person’s habitual talk about the absent is a more reliable index of character than his public moralising. The idea that inner character leaks out through small, unguarded habits is common to many ethical traditions, and it sharpens the chapter’s treatment of hypocrisy begun in 182. Valluvar implicitly invites the listener to read people by what they say about others when those others are not present.

tamil:
பிறன்பழி கூறுவான் தன்பழி யுள்ளும்
திறன்தெரிந்து கூறப் படும்.
transliteration:
Piranpazhi kooruvaan thanpazhi yullum,
Thirantherindhu koorap padum.
current_meaning: The one who spreads others’ faults will have his own faults hunted out, and the worst of them picked and told about him in turn.
elementary_explanation: If you tell everyone about your friend’s mistakes, soon people start looking for your mistakes too — and they’ll pick the most embarrassing ones to share. Gossip is like a boomerang: it comes back to hit you.
university_explanation: The couplet states a law of reciprocity in the economy of reputation. Piṟaṉ paḻi kūṟuvāṉ (“one who speaks another’s blame”) will find that taṉ paḻi uḷḷum (“even among his own blameworthy deeds”) the ones chosen with discernment (tiṟaṉ terintu) will be spoken of. The phrase tiṟaṉ terintu is sharp: people will not merely repeat his faults but select the most damaging, just as the backbiter selected and polished the faults of others. Valluvar therefore presents slander as self-defeating — by making fault-finding normal, the slanderer licenses the same treatment of himself. The passive kūṟappaṭum (“will be spoken”) leaves the agent unspecified, allowing both a social reading (others will retaliate) and a moral-causal one akin to karma. The idea that judgment returns in the same measure is widely shared across ethical traditions.

tamil:
பகச்சொல்லிக் கேளிர்ப் பிரிப்பர் நகச்சொல்லி
நட்பாடல் தேற்றா தவர்.
transliteration:
Pagachchollik kelirp pirippar nagachcholli,
Natpaadal thetraa thavar.
current_meaning: Those who do not know how to build friendship through pleasant, cheerful talk will speak words that divide people, and drive apart even their own close friends and kin.
elementary_explanation: Some people know how to make friends by saying kind, fun things. Others only know how to say “Did you hear what she said about you?” — and that makes friends fight. This kural says people who can’t make friends with nice words end up breaking friendships with nasty ones.
university_explanation: The verse is built on the chiastic pair paka-c-colli (“speaking so as to split”) and naka-c-colli (“speaking so as to make [people] laugh/rejoice”). Valluvar diagnoses divisive speech as a failure of social skill as much as of morality: those who cannot tēṟṟu (be sure of, master) the art of naṭpāṭal, friendship-making through genial conversation, fall back on the easier currency of tale-bearing. The object kēḷir means kin or intimates, so the damage falls on the speaker’s own circle — Parimelazhagar notes they alienate even their friends from themselves. This connects the chapter to the book’s later treatment of friendship (naṭpu, chapters 79–83) and recalls the Buddhist category of pisuṇā vācā, speech that splits people apart. The couplet implies a positive programme: cultivate the speech that unites, and the temptation to divide loses its hold.

tamil:
துன்னியார் குற்றமும் தூற்றும் மரபினார்
என்னைகொல் ஏதிலார் மாட்டு.
transliteration:
Thunniyaar kutramum thootrum marabinaar,
Ennaikol ethilaar maattu.
current_meaning: If people make a habit of broadcasting the faults even of those closest to them, what won’t they do to strangers?
elementary_explanation: If someone spreads secrets about their own best friend, imagine what they’d say about you! This kural says: watch how people talk about their closest friends — that’s how they’ll treat everyone else.
university_explanation: The couplet argues a fortiori from intimacy. Tuṉṉiyār (“those who are close”) are the people whom affection, obligation, and self-interest should all protect; if the slanderer’s marapu (settled disposition, habit) leads him to tūṟṟu (scatter abroad, as chaff is winnowed) even their faults, then no restraint can be expected toward ētilār, those who are unconnected to him. The rhetorical question ennaikol (“what indeed?”) leaves the outcome to the listener’s imagination. Valluvar is making a practical point about trust: how a person speaks of his intimates is the best predictor of how he will treat everyone else. The verse also implies that backbiting is not an occasional lapse but a trait, marapu, which, once formed, spares no one.

tamil:
அறன்நோக்கி ஆற்றுங்கொல் வையம் புறன்நோக்கிப்
புன்சொல் உரைப்பான் பொறை.
transliteration:
Arannokki aatrungol vaiyam purannokkip,
Punsol uraippaan porai.
current_meaning: Is it only out of regard for virtue that the earth still bears the weight of the man who waits until someone is gone and then speaks mean words about him?
elementary_explanation: The ground holds up everyone who walks on it — good people and mean people. This kural jokes that the Earth must be very patient and kind to keep carrying a gossip who waits for people to leave so he can say nasty things about them.
university_explanation: The couplet is one of Valluvar’s sharpest ironies. Vaiyam, the earth, is imagined as a moral agent who bears (āṟṟu) the poṟai (burden, weight) of the slanderer, and the poet wonders whether it does so only aṟaṉ nōkki — out of regard for dharma, since bearing all beings is its duty. The mirrored phrases aṟaṉ nōkki and puṟaṉ nōkki are carefully placed: the earth looks toward virtue, while the slanderer looks toward the back, watching for his victim’s absence before he speaks puṉ col, base words. The image draws on the Indian idea of the earth as the patient bearer of all beings, whose forbearance (poṟai also means patience) contrasts with the slanderer’s impatience to wound. Valluvar thus makes the slanderer a dead weight on the world, tolerated only by a patience he does not deserve.

tamil:
ஏதிலார் குற்றம்போல் தங்குற்றங் காண்கிற்பின்
தீதுண்டோ மன்னும் உயிர்க்கு.
transliteration:
Ethilaar kutrampol thankutrang kaankirpin,
Theedhundo mannum uyirkku.
current_meaning: If people could see their own faults as clearly as they see the faults of others, could any harm come to living beings?
elementary_explanation: It’s easy to notice when a friend makes a mistake, but hard to notice our own. If everyone checked their own mistakes as carefully as they check others’, there would be much less gossip — and much less trouble for everyone.
university_explanation: Valluvar closes the chapter by moving from prohibition to cure. The comparison ētilār kuṟṟampōl (“like the faults of strangers”) captures the ease and even pleasure with which we see others’ failings; if that same clear sight were turned on taṉ kuṟṟam, one’s own faults, the rhetorical question asks, would any harm (tītu) remain for mannum uyir — beings who endure, or, in some commentaries, the soul that persists? The logic is psychological: backbiting feeds on an asymmetry of attention, and self-examination removes both the motive and the moral standing for it. Mu. Karunanidhi’s gloss draws out the practical point — the habit of slander disappears and life becomes peaceful. The ending thus turns the chapter’s condemnation of the slanderer into a discipline for the reader, echoing a strikingly wide range of traditions that contrast the tiny flaw in others with the large one in oneself.

tamil:
பல்லார் முனியப் பயனில சொல்லுவான்
எல்லாரும் எள்ளப் படும்.
transliteration:
Pallaar muniyap payanila solluvaan,
Ellaarum ellap padum.
current_meaning: A person who keeps pouring out useless talk until many listeners are fed up with him ends up being looked down on by everyone.
elementary_explanation: Imagine someone in class who keeps talking and talking about nothing while everyone is trying to listen to the teacher. Soon nobody wants to sit next to them. This kural says that people who chatter about useless things make everyone tired of them, and then everyone stops respecting them.
university_explanation: The chapter opens with a social rather than a metaphysical sanction: the idle talker is punished by the listening community itself. The verb முனிய (muniya, “to be vexed, to loathe”) names the listeners’ reaction, and எள்ளப்படும் (ellappadum, “will be scorned”) names the outcome, so the couplet traces a causal chain from speech to irritation to contempt. The contrast of பல்லார் (“the many” who hear him) with எல்லாரும் (“everyone”) is deliberate: annoyance starts with the immediate audience but reputation spreads to the whole world. Coming straight after the chapter on backbiting (புறங்கூறாமை), the kural widens the ethics of speech from malicious words to merely empty ones, treating wasted words as a real, if quieter, wrong. Plutarch’s essay on garrulousness makes the same diagnosis, that the chatterer seeks affection and wins hatred.

tamil:
பயனில பல்லார்முன் சொல்லல் நயனில
நட்டார்கண் செய்தலிற் றீது.
transliteration:
Payanila pallaarmun sollal nayanila,
Nattaarkan seydhalir reedhu.
current_meaning: Talking pointless nonsense in front of many people is worse than doing unkind things to your own friends.
elementary_explanation: If you are rude to one friend, that hurts one person. But if you stand up in front of the whole school and waste everyone’s time with silly talk, you hurt everyone’s time at once. This kural says doing that in front of many people is even worse than being unkind to a friend.
university_explanation: The couplet works through a startling comparison. Doing நயனில (nayanila, “what is devoid of goodness/propriety”) to நட்டார் (nattaar, “friends”), which is a real ethical fault, is ranked below speaking பயனில (payanila, “what is devoid of benefit”) before பல்லார் (“the many”). The two phrases rhyme (nayanila / payanila), and the parallel sound makes the ranking stick in the ear. The argument depends on scale and publicity: an unkind act toward a friend stays in a private relationship that can be repaired, while empty talk before an assembly wastes the attention of many people at once and fixes one’s public character. Modern commentators (Mu. Varadarasan, Solomon Pappaiah, Kalaignar) all keep this ‘worse than’ reading, which shows how seriously Valluvar takes the public squandering of speech.

tamil:
நயனிலன் என்பது சொல்லும் பயனில
பாரித் துரைக்கும் உரை.
transliteration:
Nayanilan enbadhu sollum payanila,
Paarith thuraikkum urai.
current_meaning: When a man spreads out long talk about worthless things, that talk itself announces to the world that he lacks goodness.
elementary_explanation: You can often tell what kind of person someone is just by listening to them. If a person keeps talking on and on about useless things, their own words are like a sign on their back that says, “I am not a good person.” They don’t even need anyone else to say it.
university_explanation: The grammar is striking: the subject of சொல்லும் (“will declare”) is the talk itself (உரை, urai), so speech bears witness against the speaker. பாரித்து (paarittu, “spreading out, amplifying”) condemns not a single slip but the habit of stretching trivial matter into long discourse. The key term நயனிலன் (nayanilan, “one without nayan”) is glossed differently by modern commentators: Mu. Varadarasan reads it as lacking virtue (aram), Solomon Pappaiah as lacking justice (neethi), and Kalaignar as simply a ‘useless person’. All of these readings agree that speech works as a public index of inner character. The same idea appears in Solon’s maxim that speech is the image of actions, and in the Buddha’s teaching that discernment is revealed through conversation.

tamil:
நயன்சாரா நன்மையின் நீக்கும் பயன்சாராப்
பண்பில்சொல் பல்லா ரகத்து.
transliteration:
Nayansaaraa nanmaiyin neekkum payansaaraap,
Panbilsol pallaa rakaththu.
current_meaning: Words that bring no benefit and have no refinement, spoken among many people, cut a person off from virtue and remove him from goodness.
elementary_explanation: Think of a garden. Every time you throw rubbish into it, the flowers have less room to grow. Rude, useless talk in front of others is like throwing rubbish into your own heart’s garden. Bit by bit, it pushes the good things out.
university_explanation: The couplet is built on two paired negatives, பயன்சாரா (“not joined to benefit”) and நயன்சாரா (“not joined to nayan”, i.e., virtue or propriety), with பண்பில் (panpil, “uncultured, graceless”) in between. The claim is about moral formation, not reputation: such speech நன்மையின் நீக்கும் (“removes one from goodness”), gradually alienating the speaker from his own better character. Mu. Varadarasan reads the result as ‘not joining with aram and being removed from good’, while Kalaignar stresses that it also destroys the listeners’ pleasure. The setting பல்லாரகத்து (“among many”) again marks public speech as the place where habits of character are formed. The same point appears in Paul’s warning that ‘vain babblings’ ‘increase unto more ungodliness’ and in the Buddha’s listing of idle chatter among unrighteous conduct.

tamil:
சீர்மை சிறப்பொடு நீங்கும் பயனில
நீர்மை யுடையார் சொலின்.
transliteration:
Seermai sirappodu neengum payanila,
Neermai yudaiyaar solin.
current_meaning: If even people of good character speak empty words, their excellence and the honour it earned them both slip away.
elementary_explanation: Imagine a famous, respected captain of a sports team. If she starts saying silly, pointless things all the time, the team slowly stops looking up to her. This kural says that even good people lose their respect if they fill the air with useless words.
university_explanation: This kural turns from the habitual babbler to the virtuous person who lapses. நீர்மையுடையார் (neermaiyudaiyaar) means those who have fine nature, literally a ‘watery’ or gentle disposition. The couplet warns that they are not immune: their சீர்மை (seermai, ‘excellence, eminence’) departs together with its சிறப்பு (sirappu, ‘honour, distinction’). Solomon Pappaiah adds ‘அப்பொழுதே’ (‘at that very moment’), stressing how suddenly the loss comes. The point is that reputation is a fragile social credit, and vain talk spends it faster than virtue earns it. Ecclesiastes’ image of dead flies spoiling the perfumer’s ointment is perhaps the closest cross-cultural parallel.

tamil:
பயனில்சொல் பாராட்டு வானை மகன்எனல்
மக்கட் பதடி யெனல்.
transliteration:
Payanilsol paaraattu vaanai makanenal,
Makkat padhadi yenal.
current_meaning: Do not call the man who delights in showing off empty words a real man; call him the chaff among human beings.
elementary_explanation: When farmers harvest rice, the good grain is kept and the light, empty husks called chaff blow away in the wind. This kural says a person who only talks empty talk is like that chaff: they look like a person on the outside, but inside there is nothing useful.
university_explanation: Valluvar here turns from consequence to classification. பாராட்டுவான் (paaraattuvaan) means one who displays, cherishes or keeps repeating; Mu. Varadarasan glosses it as ‘saying many times’. The one who does this with பயனில்சொல் (empty words) is denied the name மகன் (makan, ‘man, human being’) and given instead மக்கட்பதடி (makkat-padhadi, ‘the chaff of humanity’). The agricultural metaphor is precise: chaff (பதர்) has the outward form of grain without its kernel, so the babbler has the form of a person without the substance that makes speech human. (One web edition prints ‘பராட்டு’ here, evidently a typo; the standard reading ‘பாராட்டு’ is followed.) The image anticipates later critiques of inauthentic ‘idle talk’, such as Heidegger’s Gerede, in which speech circulates without anyone really grasping what it is about.

tamil:
நயனில சொல்லினுஞ் சொல்லுக சான்றோர்
பயனில சொல்லாமை நன்று.
transliteration:
Nayanila sollinum solluka saandror,
Payanila sollaamai nandru.
current_meaning: The worthy may, if they must, say things that are not pleasing; but it is good for them never to say things that are useless.
elementary_explanation: A good coach may sometimes say something that stings, like “You need to practise harder!” That isn’t nice to hear, but it helps. What a good coach should never do is waste the team’s time with pointless chatter. This kural says: a hard word that helps is okay, but a useless word is not.
university_explanation: This is the chapter’s most philosophically daring couplet, because it ranks the two standards of speech against each other. நயனில (nayanila) is glossed by Kalaignar as ‘not sweet or pleasant’, by Pappaiah as ‘unjust’ and by Mu. Varadarasan as ‘lacking aram’. On the milder reading, Valluvar concedes that the சான்றோர் (saandror, the noble or accomplished) may speak unpleasantly, but insists that they must never speak uselessly. So usefulness (பயன்) is made the non-negotiable floor of speech, and pleasantness (நயன்) is a desirable but negotiable quality. This differs from Manu’s well-known rule against ‘disagreeable truth’, and it lines up closely with the Buddha’s criteria in the Abhaya Sutta, where beneficial but unwelcome words may be spoken at the right time and unbeneficial words never.

tamil:
அரும்பயன் ஆயும் அறிவினார் சொல்லார்
பெரும்பயன் இல்லாத சொல்.
transliteration:
Arumpayan aayum arivinaar sollaar,
Perumpayan illaadha sol.
current_meaning: Wise people who search out rare and precious benefits never speak words that do not carry great benefit.
elementary_explanation: If you are hunting for gold, you don’t fill your bag with ordinary pebbles. Wise people are like gold-hunters with their words: they only say things that are really valuable, and they don’t waste words on things that don’t matter.
university_explanation: The couplet raises the standard. It is not enough for words to have some பயன் (benefit): the wise refuse words lacking பெரும்பயன் (perumpayan, ‘great benefit’). The rhyme of அரும்பயன் (arumpayan, ‘rare benefit’) with பெரும்பயன் binds the two halves together: those who investigate (ஆயும், aayum) rare and valuable ends apply the same selectiveness to their own speech. This describes an intellectual temperament as much as an ethical rule, since the discerning mind that weighs what is worth pursuing also weighs what is worth saying. The Upanishadic command to ‘leave off other words’, Shammai’s ‘speak little’ and Homer’s portrait of Menelaus as ‘a man of few words’ all praise the same economy of speech.

tamil:
பொருள்தீர்ந்த பொச்சாந்துஞ் சொல்லார் மருள்தீர்ந்த
மாசறு காட்சி யவர்.
transliteration:
Poruldheerndha pochchaandhum sollaar maruldheerndha,
Maasaru kaatchi yavar.
current_meaning: Those whose vision is spotless and free of delusion will not speak meaningless words, not even by a slip of forgetfulness.
elementary_explanation: Some people are so careful and clear-headed that even when they are tired or distracted, they don’t blurt out silly things. This kural says that people whose minds are truly clean and clear don’t say empty words even by accident.
university_explanation: The couplet balances two phrases built on தீர்ந்த (theerndha, ‘ended, freed of’). The speech is பொருள்தீர்ந்த (‘emptied of meaning’), and the speakers are மருள்தீர்ந்த (‘freed of delusion’). The symmetry suggests that meaningless words can only come from a mind that still holds some confusion. பொச்சாந்தும் (pochchaandhum, ‘even through forgetfulness/heedlessness’) raises the standard from deliberate restraint to spontaneous purity: the மாசறு காட்சியவர் (maasaru kaatchiyavar, ‘those of flawless insight’) do not need to police their tongues, because nothing empty is left in them to come out. Pochchaappu (heedlessness) later gets a chapter of its own (ch. 54, பொச்சாவாமை), which shows how central vigilance is to Valluvar’s ethics. There is a close parallel in the Buddhist portrait of the freed person whose ‘speech is calm’ and in James’s ‘perfect man’ who ‘offends not in word’.

tamil:
சொல்லுக சொல்லிற் பயனுடைய சொல்லற்க
சொல்லிற் பயனிலாச் சொல்.
transliteration:
Solluka sollir payanudaiya sollarka,
Sollir payanilaach sol.
current_meaning: Of all the words you could say, speak only those that are useful; of all the words you could say, never speak those that are useless.
elementary_explanation: Before you speak, ask yourself one simple question: “Will this help?” If the answer is yes, say it. If the answer is no, don’t. That’s the whole rule, and this kural says it in the simplest way possible.
university_explanation: The chapter closes with one of the most famous sound-patterns in the Kural. Forms of சொல் (sol, ‘word/speak’) occur five times: சொல்லுக (‘speak’), சொல்லில் (‘among words’, twice), சொல்லற்க (‘do not speak’) and சொல் (‘word’). The only thing that changes between the positive and negative halves is பயனுடைய / பயனிலா (‘useful / useless’). The form enacts the content: a couplet made almost entirely of the word ‘word’ shows perfect economy, with nothing wasted. Solomon Pappaiah reads பயன் as the three classical aims of life (aram, porul, inbam), which ties the rule to the whole structure of the Kural. The maxim sums up the chapter as a single test that can be applied to every utterance, much like Epictetus’s ‘speak merely what is necessary’ and the hadith ‘speak good or keep quiet’.

tamil:
தீவினையார் அஞ்சார் விழுமியார் அஞ்சுவர்
தீவினை என்னும் செருக்கு.
transliteration:
Theevinaiyaar anjaar vizhumiyaar anjuvar,
Theevinai ennum serukku.
current_meaning: Those already steeped in wrongdoing feel no fear of the heady arrogance that evil deeds bring; only the truly noble are afraid of it.
elementary_explanation: Imagine two kids near a hot stove. One has touched it so many times he doesn’t even flinch anymore. The other is careful and keeps her hands away. This kural says good people are like the careful kid — they are scared of doing bad things, while people who do bad things all the time have stopped being scared at all.
university_explanation: Valluvar opens the chapter with a paradox: fear, usually a mark of weakness, is here the mark of excellence (விழுமியார், “the eminent”). The object of dread is not punishment but “the pride called evil-doing” (தீவினை என்னும் செருக்கு) — Parimelazhagar reads செருக்கு as the intoxication or swagger that evil deeds produce, which dulls conscience the more one indulges it. The couplet thus describes moral desensitization: habitual wrongdoers lose the very faculty of dread that protects the noble. This anticipates what Buddhist ethics calls hiri-ottappa (moral shame and moral dread) and Jewish ethics calls yirat cheit (fear of sin) — fear reconceived as a moral sense rather than cowardice.

tamil:
தீயவை தீய பயத்தலால் தீயவை
தீயினும் அஞ்சப் படும்.
transliteration:
Theeyavai theeya payaththalaal theeyavai,
Theeyinum anjap padum.
current_meaning: Because evil deeds give rise to further evil, they should be feared even more than fire.
elementary_explanation: Fire can burn you, so you keep away from it. But a bad deed is even worse than fire — one bad deed leads to another bad deed, and then another, like sparks starting more fires. So we should be even more careful about doing bad things than about touching fire.
university_explanation: The couplet is built on a deliberate pun: தீ means both “evil” and “fire,” and தீயவை (“evil things”) sounds like “fiery things.” Valluvar’s argument is comparative — fire burns only what it touches and can be put out, but evil propagates, generating consequences for both the victim and the doer (Pulavar Kesigan: ‘to others and to oneself’). Evil is therefore self-replicating in a way fire only resembles. The same insight — that wrongdoing breeds more wrongdoing — appears in the rabbinic dictum that ‘one transgression leads to another’ and in Aeschylus’s image of the evil deed that begets its own offspring.

tamil:
அறிவினுள் எல்லாந் தலையென்ப தீய
செறுவார்க்கும் செய்யா விடல்.
transliteration:
Arivinul ellaan thalaiyenba theeya,
Seruvaarkkum seyyaa vidal.
current_meaning: The wise say that the highest of all wisdom is to refrain from doing evil even to those who harm us.
elementary_explanation: If someone knocks down your sandcastle, you might want to knock down theirs. But the smartest thing — smarter than anything in any book — is to not do something bad back. Being kind even to someone who was mean to you is the cleverest thing of all.
university_explanation: Here Valluvar relocates the virtue of non-retaliation from the realm of emotion (forgiveness) into the realm of intellect: it is the ‘head’ (தலை) of all knowledge. செறுவார் means those who actively hurt or oppress one — genuine enemies, not mere irritants. The claim is that true intelligence sees what the vengeful cannot: that returning evil only multiplies it (the logic of 202) and binds the retaliator to the same consequences. The idea stands in striking agreement with Socrates in the Crito, who argues on rational grounds that one must never return wrong for wrong.

tamil:
மறந்தும் பிறன்கேடு சூழற்க சூழின்
அறஞ்சூழும் சூழ்ந்தவன் கேடு.
transliteration:
Marandhum pirankedu soozharka soozhin,
Aransoozhum soozhndhavan kedu.
current_meaning: Do not plot another’s ruin even absent-mindedly; if you do, Virtue itself will plot the ruin of the one who plotted.
elementary_explanation: It’s like throwing a boomerang at someone — it comes flying back at you. This kural says even thinking up a plan to hurt someone is like that boomerang: goodness itself will turn the plan around so it lands on you.
university_explanation: The verb சூழ் (‘to plan, surround, encompass’) is repeated three times, mirroring the plot and counter-plot: the schemer ‘surrounds’ another’s ruin, and Aram (Virtue, personified by Solomon Pappaiah as அறக்கடவுள், the deity of Virtue) ‘surrounds’ the schemer’s ruin in turn. Note the extreme standard set by மறந்தும் (‘even in forgetfulness’): not merely the deed but even a passing intention to harm is forbidden. The textual tradition is worth noting — Project Madurai and thirukkural.net print அறஞ்சூழம், but the standard reading followed by commentators and kuraltheni.com is அறஞ்சூழும் (‘will plot’). The ‘plot that recoils on the plotter’ is a near-universal motif, from Haman’s gallows to Hesiod’s ‘evil planned harms the plotter most’.

tamil:
இலன்என்று தீயவை செய்யற்க செய்யின்
இலனாகும் மற்றும் பெயர்த்து.
transliteration:
Ilan endru theeyavai seyyarka seyyin,
Ilanaagum matrum peyarththu.
current_meaning: Do not commit evil on the excuse that you are poor; if you do, you will only become poorer still.
elementary_explanation: Suppose you have no snacks and you take someone else’s lunch. Now nobody trusts you, nobody shares with you, and you might get in big trouble. You end up with even less than before! Being poor is never a good reason to do bad things — it just makes things worse.
university_explanation: Valluvar anticipates the most sympathetic excuse for wrongdoing — need — and refuses it. இலன் (‘one who has not’) is echoed in the second line (இலனாகும், ‘becomes one who has not’) with பெயர்த்து (‘again, once more’), producing a circular structure that mirrors the poverty trap itself: evil committed to escape want returns one to want. Most commentators (Mu. Varadarasan, Pappaiah, Kalaignar) read இலன் as ‘poor’; Pulavar Kesigan offers an alternative — ‘do not harm someone because he is without support’ — which shifts the focus to exploiting the weak. On the dominant reading, the couplet makes a hard-headed point: ill-gotten means destroy trust, reputation and future prosperity, and so perpetuate the very lack they were meant to cure.

tamil:
தீப்பால தான்பிறர்கண் செய்யற்க நோய்ப்பால
தன்னை அடல்வேண்டா தான்.
transliteration:
Theeppaala thaanpirarkan seyyarka noippaala,
Thannai adalvendaa thaan.
current_meaning: Whoever does not wish to be tormented by suffering should never do evil to others.
elementary_explanation: If you don’t want anyone to pull your hair, don’t pull anyone else’s hair. This kural says: if you don’t want bad things to happen to you, don’t do bad things to other people.
university_explanation: The couplet is built on a pair of parallel compounds — தீப்பால (‘things of the evil kind’) done to others, and நோய்ப்பால (‘things of the suffering kind’) that might afflict oneself — so that the grammar itself enacts reciprocity. Commentators agree the sense is causal: suffering that ‘attacks’ (அடல்) a person is the return of the evil he has done. The argument is prudential and universal — anyone who does not want pain has a reason not to inflict it — which makes this Valluvar’s version of the negative Golden Rule. That rule appears independently in the Mahabharata, in Hillel, in Isocrates, in the Buddha and in the Gospels, one of the most striking convergences in world ethics.

tamil:
எனைப்பகை யுற்றாரும் உய்வர் வினைப்பகை
வீயாது பின்சென்று அடும்.
transliteration:
Enaippakai yutraarum uyvar vinaippakai,
Veeyaadhu pinsendru adum.
current_meaning: People can survive any enmity, however great; but the enmity of their own evil deeds never dies — it follows them and destroys them.
elementary_explanation: You can hide from a bully, run away, or make friends again. But the bad things you did are like a shadow-monster that follows you everywhere. You can’t hide from it or run away from it, because it comes from you.
university_explanation: The contrast is between பகை (enmity) from others and வினைப்பகை (‘the enmity of deeds’) — Valluvar’s striking personification of karma as a relentless personal foe. Human enemies can be escaped, appeased or outlived (உய்வர், ‘they survive’); the enemy that is one’s own past action ‘does not perish’ (வீயாது), ‘goes behind’ (பின்சென்று) and ‘kills’ (அடும்). The image of pursuit is shared with the Greek Erinyes, who hound Orestes across the world, and with the Mahabharata’s calf that unfailingly finds its mother among a thousand cows. The couplet thus answers a common hope of wrongdoers — that they might outrun consequences.

tamil:
தீயவை செய்தார் கெடுதல் நிழல்தன்னை
வீயாது அடிஉறைந் தற்று.
transliteration:
Theeyavai seydhaar kedudhal nizhaldhannai,
Veeyaadhu adiyuraindh thatru.
current_meaning: Ruin clings to those who do evil just as a person’s shadow never leaves him but stays right at his feet.
elementary_explanation: Try running away from your shadow — you can’t! It sticks to your feet wherever you go. This kural says trouble sticks to people who do bad things in the same way. It follows them everywhere.
university_explanation: Valluvar sharpens the pursuit image of 207 into a simile of inseparability: the shadow does not merely follow but ‘dwells at the feet’ (அடியுறை) — the phrase also evokes a servant or dependent who lives at one’s feet. A shadow is produced by the person himself, so the image implies that ruin is not an external punishment but a by-product of one’s own action, as inseparable as it is self-generated. The text itself shows a scribal wrinkle: Project Madurai and thirukkural.net read ‘அஇஉறைந்’, an evident typographical corruption; ytamizh.com and kuruvirotti.com give அடிஉறைந் (‘dwelling at the feet’), the reading adopted here. The shadow simile famously also appears in the second verse of the Dhammapada, but applied to good deeds.

tamil:
தன்னைத்தான் காதல னாயின் எனைத்தொன்றும்
துன்னற்க தீவினைப் பால்.
transliteration:
Thannaiththaan kaadhala naayin enaiththondrum,
Thunnarka theevinaip paal.
current_meaning: If a person truly loves himself, let him not go near evil of any kind, however small.
elementary_explanation: If you love yourself, you take care of yourself — you brush your teeth and wear a helmet on your bike. This kural says that taking care of yourself also means staying away from bad deeds, even tiny ones, because they end up hurting you.
university_explanation: Valluvar here turns self-love (தன்னைத்தான் காதலன்) — often treated as a vice — into the very motive for virtue: anyone who genuinely wishes himself well will keep away from evil. The key intensifier is எனைத்தொன்றும் (‘any whatsoever, however slight’), and the verb துன்னற்க means ‘do not approach or come near’, implying avoidance of the whole territory of evil (தீவினைப் பால், ‘the side/portion of evil’) rather than only its grave acts. This is a form of ‘enlightened self-interest’: properly understood, self-love and morality coincide. Aristotle makes the same argument in Nicomachean Ethics IX.8, and the Dhammapada puts it in almost the same words: ‘If one holds oneself dear, one should diligently watch oneself.’

tamil:
அருங்கேடன் என்பது அறிக மருங்கோடித்
தீவினை செய்யான் எனின்.
transliteration:
Arungedan enbadhu arika marungodith,
Theevinai seyyaan enin.
current_meaning: Know that a person who never strays from the right path to do evil is safe from ruin.
