வஞ்ச மனத்தான் படிற்றொழுக்கம் பூதங்கள்
ஐந்தும் அகத்தே நகும்.
transliteration:
Vanja manaththaan padittrozhukkam boodhangal
Aindhum agaththe nagum.
current_meaning: When a man with a deceitful mind puts on a false show of holy conduct, the five elements that make up his own body laugh at him from within.
elementary_explanation: Imagine someone pretending to be very good while secretly cheating. People outside might be fooled, but the earth, water, fire, air and sky that his body is made of can see everything — and they giggle at the silly act. You can’t hide a lie from the stuff you are made of.
university_explanation: The chapter opens with a striking image: the five great elements (pancha bhutas — earth, water, fire, air, ether) that compose the hypocrite’s body are themselves the witnesses who see through his sham piety and laugh inwardly. The word படிற்றொழுக்கம் (padittrozhukkam) denotes counterfeit or disguised conduct, and அகத்தே (agaththe) plays on “inside” — both inside the body and inside themselves. The point is that concealment is metaphysically impossible: the deceiver carries his witnesses with him. Parimelazhagar’s tradition reads the elements’ laughter as mockery of a man who thinks he can fool the world while his own substance knows the truth — a theme paralleled by Manu’s list of cosmic witnesses and the Qur’anic image of skins testifying.

tamil:
வானுயர் தோற்றம் எவன்செய்யும் தன்னெஞ்சம்
தான்அறி குற்றப் படின்.
transliteration:
Vaanuyar thotram evanseyyum thannenjam
Thaanari kutrap padin.
current_meaning: What good is an appearance of holiness as high as the sky, if a man’s own heart is sunk in faults that he himself knows about?
elementary_explanation: Suppose you wear a shiny superhero costume, but inside you know you just took your friend’s toy without asking. The costume doesn’t make you a hero. What you know about yourself matters more than how you look.
university_explanation: வானுயர் தோற்றம் (“a sky-high appearance”) refers to the imposing garb and bearing of the ascetic, and Valluvar poses a rhetorical question: of what use is it? The criterion he sets is not public exposure but self-knowledge — தன்னெஞ்சம் தான் அறி குற்றம், the fault the heart itself is aware of. Valluvar thus locates moral judgement in conscience rather than reputation, a remarkably interior standard for an ancient ethical text. The kural parallels the Gita’s notion of mithyācāra (the pretender whose mind dwells on what his outward restraint pretends to renounce), and Stoic ideas of conscience as the one witness who cannot be deceived.

tamil:
வலியில் நிலைமையான் வல்லுருவம் பெற்றம்
புலியின்தோல் போர்த்துமேய்ந் தற்று.
transliteration:
Valiyil nilaimaiyaan valluruvam petram
Puliyinthol porththumeindh thatru.
current_meaning: A man without the inner strength to master his senses who puts on the stern appearance of an ascetic is like a cow grazing on crops while wrapped in a tiger’s skin.
elementary_explanation: Picture a cow wearing a tiger costume so it can sneak into a farm and eat the crops. It looks scary, but it’s still just a cow munching grass. A person who dresses like a strong holy person but can’t control himself is the same — a costume on the outside, the same old habits inside.
university_explanation: The simile is doubly pointed: the cow is weak, not fierce, and the tiger-skin lends it a borrowed terror that lets it graze unchallenged on another’s field. வலியில் நிலைமையான் (“one lacking the strength” — traditionally, strength to restrain the senses) contrasts with வல்லுருவம் (“a mighty form”), the forbidding garb of tapas. The target is not ordinary weakness but the exploitation of a sacred appearance to feed appetite. The same fable circulated widely in the ancient world — the Panchatantra’s ass in the tiger-skin and Aesop’s ass in the lion’s skin — and in both the disguise ultimately betrays itself.

tamil:
தவமறைந்து அல்லவை செய்தல் புதல்மறைந்து
வேட்டுவன் புள்சிமிழ்த் தற்று.
transliteration:
Thavamaraindhu allavai seydhal pudhalmaraindhu
Vettuvan pulsimizhth thatru.
current_meaning: To hide behind the garb of penance and commit wrongs is like a hunter who hides behind a bush to snare birds.
elementary_explanation: A bird hunter hides in a bush so the birds think it’s just a plant, and then — snap! — he catches them. Someone who pretends to be holy so people trust him, and then tricks them, is doing the same thing. The holy look is just his hiding bush.
university_explanation: Valluvar here turns from the hypocrite’s inner weakness to his active predation. The verb மறைந்து (“hiding”) appears twice in parallel — தவம் மறைந்து / புதல் மறைந்து — making tapas itself the thicket, the camouflage that renders the trapper invisible to his prey. The trusting public are the birds (புள்), drawn close precisely because the cover looks harmless and natural. This anticipates the widespread Indian motif of the “cat-ascetic” (baiḍāla-vratika) who adopts vows to lure victims — condemned in both the Mahabharata and Manu — and resonates with Jesus’ charge that the Pharisees ‘for a pretence make long prayer’ while devouring widows’ houses.

tamil:
பற்றற்றேம் என்பார் படிற்றொழுக்கம் எற்றெற்றென்று
ஏதம் பலவுந் தரும்.
transliteration:
Patratrem enbaar padittrozhukkam etretrendru
Edham palavum tharum.
current_meaning: The false conduct of those who claim, “We have renounced all attachment,” will bring them many sorrows that make them cry out, “What have we done! What have we done!”
elementary_explanation: If you tell everyone you gave up sweets, but secretly eat them all, one day you’ll be caught — and you’ll feel terrible and say, “Why did I do that?” Pretending costs more in the end than being honest.
university_explanation: The kural records the hypocrite’s own claim — பற்றற்றேம் (“we are free of attachment”) — and sets against it his eventual cry, எற்று எற்று (“what [have we done], what!”), an onomatopoeic doubled lament unusual in the Kural. Valluvar’s focus is on consequences: படிற்றொழுக்கம் (disguised conduct) produces ஏதம் பலவும், “many evils,” culminating in bitter self-reproach. The phrase may refer both to worldly ruin when the imposture is exposed and to karmic suffering afterwards. The pattern — pretended renunciation leading to anguished regret — is echoed in Manu’s consignment of ‘cat’ and ‘heron’ ascetics to hell and in Jesus’ ‘weeping and gnashing of teeth’ for hypocrites.

tamil:
நெஞ்சின் துறவார் துறந்தார்போல் வஞ்சித்து
வாழ்வாரின் வன்கணார் இல்.
transliteration:
Nenjin thuravaar thurandhaarpol vanjiththu
Vaazhvaarin vankanaar il.
current_meaning: There are none more hard-hearted than those who have not renounced in their hearts, yet live by deceiving others while posing as renunciants.
elementary_explanation: Some people pretend to be kind helpers who need nothing, so others trust them and give them things — but secretly they are greedy. Valluvar says that tricking people who trust you like this is about the meanest thing a person can do.
university_explanation: Valluvar’s strongest verdict in the chapter uses வன்கணார் — literally “the hard-eyed,” those without compassion — and makes it superlative: none are worse (இல்). The contrast நெஞ்சின் துறவார் / துறந்தார்போல் (“not renounced in heart” / “like those who renounced”) sharpens the gap between inner reality and outward role. The special cruelty lies in exploiting the reverence and generosity that society extends to genuine renunciants, and so corrupting the very institution of trust. Plato made the same ranking when Adeimantus and Glaucon called seeming-just-while-being-unjust the ‘highest reach’ of injustice, and Manu classes such pretenders as ‘cats’ bent on doing injury.

tamil:
புறங்குன்றி கண்டனைய ரேனும் அகங்குன்றி
முக்கிற் கரியார் உடைத்து.
transliteration:
Purangundri kandanaiya renum agangundri
Mukkir kariyaar udaiththu.
current_meaning: The world has people who look as bright and red outside as the kundri (jequirity) seed, yet inside are as black as the seed’s dark tip.
elementary_explanation: There’s a tiny seed that is shiny red all over — except for one small black spot. Some people are like that: they look bright and good on the outside, but they hide a dark spot inside. Don’t judge only by the shiny part.
university_explanation: The kundri (குன்றி, Abrus precatorius) is a brilliant scarlet seed with a black spot at its ‘nose’ (மூக்கு); Valluvar makes it an emblem of the hypocrite, crimson-bright in outward piety, black at the core. The line plays on the repeated குன்றி in புறம் (outer) and அகம் (inner) — the fundamental Tamil poetic pair — so that the seed embodies both states at once. The seed was also used as a jeweller’s weight and is poisonous, which adds a latent irony: something small, attractive and valued conceals toxicity. The image anticipates Jesus’ ‘whited sepulchres’ and Hesiod’s Pandora — beauty outside, deceit within.

tamil:
மனத்தது மாசாக மாண்டார் நீராடி
மறைந்தொழுகு மாந்தர் பலர்.
transliteration:
Manaththadhu maasaaga maandaar neeraadi
Maraindhozhugu maandhar palar.
current_meaning: Many are the people who, with filth in their minds, bathe in sacred waters as though they were great souls, and live hidden behind that show.
elementary_explanation: Taking a bath gets the dirt off your skin — but it can’t wash away a mean or dishonest thought. Some people make a big show of holy bathing so everyone thinks they’re pure, but inside they’re still dirty. Clean hands don’t mean a clean heart.
university_explanation: Ritual bathing (நீராடல்) was the most visible sign of purity in both Brahmanical and Tamil religious life; Valluvar turns it into an instrument of concealment. The phrase மாண்டார் நீராடி can be read ‘bathing like the great (மாண்டார்)’ — imitating the ablutions of true sages — and மறைந்தொழுகு (‘conduct in hiding’) suggests that the water itself becomes a screen, as Kalaignar’s gloss has it: submerged, the bather disappears. The mind (மனம்) is the site of மாசு (impurity), echoing Kural 34’s definition of dharma as a mind free of stain. Across traditions, from Isaiah’s ‘Wash you, make you clean’ to Heraclitus mocking blood-purification, the same protest is made: outward ablution cannot cleanse inward defilement.

tamil:
கணைகொடிது யாழ்கோடு செவ்விதுஆங் கன்ன
வினைபடு பாலால் கொளல்.
transliteration:
Kanaikodidhu yaazhkodu sevvidhuaang kanna
Vinaipadu paalaal kolal.
current_meaning: The arrow, though straight, is cruel; the lute, though its neck is bent, is sweet. In the same way, judge people by the nature of their deeds, not by how they look.
elementary_explanation: An arrow looks perfectly straight, but it’s made for hurting. A guitar has a curvy neck, but it makes lovely music. So don’t decide who is good just by how they look — watch what they actually do.
university_explanation: Here Valluvar moves from condemnation to method: how can one tell the hypocrite from the saint? The paired images turn the usual metaphors upside down — கணை (arrow) is straight yet கொடிது (cruel), while யாழ்கோடு (the curved neck of the yazh, the ancient Tamil harp-lute) is bent yet செவ்விது (upright, good). Since செம்மை and கொடுமை mean both ‘straight/crooked’ and ‘good/cruel’, the kural exploits the double meaning to show that visual straightness and moral straightness are different things. The conclusion — வினைபடு பாலால் கொளல், ‘assess by the quality of deeds’ — is a pragmatic epistemology of character that parallels Jesus’ ‘by their fruits ye shall know them’ and the Yaksha’s answer that conduct, not birth or learning, makes a Brahmin.

tamil:
மழித்தலும் நீட்டலும் வேண்டா உலகம்
பழித்தது ஒழித்து விடின்.
transliteration:
Mazhiththalum neettalum vendaa ulagam
Pazhiththadhu ozhiththu vidin.
current_meaning: There is no need to shave the head or to grow the hair long, if one simply gives up what the world condemns as wrong.
elementary_explanation: Some holy people shave their heads and some grow their hair really long. Valluvar says: your haircut doesn’t make you good! If you stop doing bad things, you’re already on the right path — hair or no hair.
university_explanation: The chapter closes with its most famous and most radical line. மழித்தல் (shaving the head, as Jain and Buddhist monks did) and நீட்டல் (growing matted locks, as Shaiva and Vedic ascetics did) were the defining visual signs of rival renunciant orders; Valluvar dismisses both in a single breath, declaring them unnecessary (வேண்டா). The only real requirement is ethical: உலகம் பழித்தது ஒழித்தல் — abandoning what the wise of the world condemn. This non-sectarian move, placing conduct above every order’s insignia, is characteristic of the Kural as a whole and parallels the Dhammapada’s dismissal of tonsure and matted hair, Manu’s ‘the external mark is not the cause of merit’, and Seneca’s warning against the philosopher’s unkempt beard.

tamil:
எள்ளாமை வேண்டுவான் என்பான் எனைத்தொன்றும்
கள்ளாமை காக்கதன் நெஞ்சு.
transliteration:
Ellaamai venduvaan enbaan enaiththondrum,
Kallaamai kaakkathan nenju.
current_meaning: Anyone who wishes never to be held in contempt must guard his own heart so that it never even plots to take, by stealth or trickery, anything at all that belongs to another, however small.
elementary_explanation: Nobody wants to be laughed at or called a cheat. The way to make sure that never happens is to keep a guard at the door of your own mind, so that even the idea of sneaking away something that isn’t yours — even a pencil — never gets in.
university_explanation: The chapter opens by locating fraud (kaḷavu) not in the hand but in the heart (neñcu): the verb is kākka, “let him guard,” and its object is the mind itself. Valluvar’s motive clause is social and reputational — eḷḷāmai, “not being scorned” — which fits the householder-and-ascetic audience of the Tuṟavaṟaviyal section, where public trust is the currency of a moral life. The word eṉaittoṉṟum (“anything whatsoever”) forecloses the familiar rationalisation that small frauds do not count, anticipating the Aristotelian claim that theft admits no virtuous mean. Commentators from Parimēlaḻakar to Mu. Varadarasan read kaḷḷāmai as covering not only burglary but every covert appropriation, including short-changing and deceit in dealings.

tamil:
உள்ளத்தால் உள்ளலும் தீதே பிறன்பொருளைக்
கள்ளத்தால் கள்வேம் எனல்.
transliteration:
Ullaththaal ullalum theethe piranporulaik,
Kallaththaal kalvem enal.
current_meaning: Even to think in one’s mind, “I will take his property from him by cunning,” is itself a wrong.
elementary_explanation: Imagine thinking, “When no one is looking, I’ll trick my friend out of his toy.” Even if you never do it, just planning it is already a bad step, because every wrong action begins as a thought.
university_explanation: Valluvar moves culpability upstream from act to intention: uḷḷattāl uḷḷalum tītē — “even the thinking with the mind is evil.” The phrase kaḷḷattāl kaḷvēm (“we shall steal by craft”) specifies the content of the forbidden thought as a deliberate scheme, not a passing temptation, which is important for the ethical claim. This parallels the Tenth Commandment’s ban on coveting, the Buddhist teaching that mind precedes action, and the Gita’s account of how dwelling on objects breeds desire. Commentators note the psychological realism: fraud requires premeditation, so the only reliable defence is to refuse the premeditation itself.

tamil:
களவினால் ஆகிய ஆக்கம் அளவிறந்து
ஆவது போலக் கெடும்.
transliteration:
Kalavinaal aakiya aakkam alavirandhu,
Aavadhu polak kedum.
current_meaning: Wealth gained through fraud may seem to swell beyond all measure, but it will perish — and take more with it than it brought.
elementary_explanation: It’s like a soap bubble: a stolen treasure puffs up bigger and bigger and looks amazing, and then — pop! — it’s gone, and it can even splash away the things you already had.
university_explanation: The couplet turns on the paradox of āvatu pōla, “as if growing”: fraudulent gain has the appearance of prosperity but not its substance. The phrase aḷaviṟantu is read two ways by commentators — as “beyond measure” describing the apparent growth, or (with Mu. Varadarasan and Kalaignar) as the ruin exceeding its natural limit and consuming even legitimately held wealth. Either way, Valluvar denies the fraudster even a prudential victory. The same instability of ill-gotten wealth is a commonplace across Hesiod, Proverbs, Jeremiah and the Qur’an, suggesting a widely shared moral-economic intuition that dishonest gain lacks durable foundations.

tamil:
களவின்கண் கன்றிய காதல் விளைவின்கண்
வீயா விழுமம் தரும்.
transliteration:
Kalavinkan kandriya kaadhal vilaivinkan,
Veeyaa vizhumam tharum.
current_meaning: An ingrained craving for gain by fraud, when it finally bears its fruit, yields sorrow that never ends.
elementary_explanation: Wanting to cheat is like planting a thorn bush because its flowers look pretty. When it grows up, the thorns keep poking you, and you can never get rid of them.
university_explanation: Kaṉṟiya kātal — a desire that has become hardened or habitual — is the subject, and the agricultural verb viḷaivu (ripening, harvest) sets up the karmic metaphor: fraud is a seed whose fruit is vīyā viḻumam, “unperishing affliction.” The emphasis on habit links this couplet to 286 and 288, where Valluvar treats fraud as a character formed by repetition. The imagery of delayed but certain ripening is close to the Dhammapada’s description of evil deeds that seem sweet until they ripen. Commentators split between reading the sorrow as this-worldly (disgrace, punishment) and as extending into later births; the adjective vīyā allows both.

tamil:
அருள்கருதி அன்புடைய ராதல் பொருள்கருதிப்
பொச்சாப்புப் பார்ப்பார்கண் இல்.
transliteration:
Arulkarudhi anbudaiya raadhal porulkarudhip,
Pochchaappup paarppaarkan il.
current_meaning: Those who covet another’s goods and wait for his moment of carelessness cannot be people of love who cherish compassion.
elementary_explanation: A real friend helps you when you drop your lunch money. Someone who waits for you to drop it so they can grab it can’t be kind at the same time — the waiting-to-grab heart pushes the kindness out.
university_explanation: The couplet contrasts two inner orientations: aruḷ karuti, “holding grace (compassion) in regard,” and poruḷ karuti, “holding another’s wealth in regard.” The fraudster’s signature act is poccāppu pārttal — watching for the other person’s forgetfulness or unguardedness — which Valluvar treats as incompatible with aṉpu (love). The couplet ties this chapter to the preceding ones on Aruḷuṭaimai (compassion), showing that for Valluvar honesty in dealings is not a separate commercial rule but a consequence of compassion. Kant’s shopkeeper, the hadith of the wet grain, and Micah’s schemers lying awake all describe the same failure: treating another person’s vulnerability as an opportunity.

tamil:
அளவின்கண் நின்றொழுகல் ஆற்றார் களவின்கண்
கன்றிய காத லவர்.
transliteration:
Alavinkan nindrozhugal aatraar kalavinkan,
Kandriya kaadha lavar.
current_meaning: Those in whom the love of gain by fraud has hardened cannot keep their conduct within the bounds of measure.
elementary_explanation: A scale in a shop is supposed to measure fairly. Someone who loves cheating is like a scale with a broken spring — it can’t stay steady, and it keeps tipping the wrong way.
university_explanation: Aḷavu (“measure, limit”) is the key term of the second half of the chapter (286-289), and Valluvar plays on its near-rhyme with kaḷavu (“fraud, theft”). Commentators differ on what aḷavu means: Parimēlaḻakar takes it as the ascetic’s limited livelihood, Mu. Varadarasan as thrift or contentment, others as the rule of right conduct. The rhyme itself makes the point that fraud is a failure of measure, which is why honest weights and measures are the concrete test in Leviticus, Deuteronomy, the Qur’an and the Buddhist suttas. The couplet repeats kaṉṟiya kātal from 284, presenting fraud as a habit that eats away the ability to keep within limits.

tamil:
களவென்னும் காரறி வாண்மை அளவென்னும்
ஆற்றல் புரிந்தார்கண் இல்.
transliteration:
Kalavennum kaarari vaanmai alavennum,
Aatral purindhaarkan il.
current_meaning: The dark cleverness called fraud is not found in those who have chosen the strength called measure.
elementary_explanation: Some people are clever in a sneaky, shadowy way. But a person who has learned to be happy with a fair share has a brighter kind of strength, and the sneaky cleverness simply has no room to live in them.
university_explanation: Kār aṟivu — literally “black knowledge” — is Valluvar’s striking name for fraud: an intelligence that is real but darkened, directed at deception rather than understanding. He opposes to it aḷavu eṉṉum āṟṟal, “the power called measure,” so that restraint is framed not as weakness but as a form of strength. The contrast anticipates Aristotle’s distinction between practical wisdom and mere cleverness (deinotēs), which can serve bad ends. Textual note: some online editions print the last word-group as புரிந்தார்கண்ட இல்; the reading புரிந்தார்கண் இல் given here follows Tamil Surangam and thirukkural-thamizh.org and fits the metre.

tamil:
அளவறிந்தார் நெஞ்சத் தறம்போல நிற்கும்
களவறிந்தார் நெஞ்சில் கரவு.
transliteration:
Alavarindhaar nenjath tharampola nirkum,
Kalavarindhaar nenjil karavu.
current_meaning: Just as virtue lives steadily in the hearts of those who know measure, deceit lives steadily in the hearts of those who have learned fraud.
elementary_explanation: Your heart is like a room. If you practise being fair, fairness moves in and makes itself at home. If you practise cheating, sneakiness moves in instead — and whoever lives there decides how you act.
university_explanation: The couplet is built on precise parallelism — aḷavu aṟintār / kaḷavu aṟintār (“those who know measure / those who know fraud”) — with the verb niṟkum (“stands, abides”) serving both halves. The point is that virtue and deceit (karavu, “concealment”) are both settled dispositions formed by what one has come to “know” through practice. This is close to Aristotle’s claim that we become just or unjust through our dealings with others, and to the Gospel image of the heart as a treasury from which good or evil is brought out. It also explains 284 and 286: once fraud is ‘known’ in this habitual sense, concealment becomes the heart’s standing condition.

tamil:
அளவல்ல செய்தாங்கே வீவர் களவல்ல
மற்றைய தேற்றா தவர்.
transliteration:
Alavalla seydhaange veevar kalavalla,
Matraiya thetraa thavar.
current_meaning: Those who know no way of living other than fraud will be destroyed in the very act of their measureless deeds.
elementary_explanation: If the only trick you know is cheating, it’s like a player who only knows how to foul — sooner or later, right in the middle of the game, they get caught and sent off.
university_explanation: The couplet says the fraudster’s ruin is not deferred but comes āṅkē — “right there,” in the act itself. The phrase kaḷavu alla maṟṟaiya tēṟṟātavar (“those who do not understand anything other than fraud”) describes a person whose repertoire has narrowed to one method, which completes the habituation argument of 288. Plato gives a striking parallel: a completely unjust person could not act at all, because cooperation depends on some remnant of justice. Acts 5’s account of Ananias, struck down while misrepresenting a sale, is the most literal illustration of perishing ‘right there.’

tamil:
கள்வார்க்குத் தள்ளும் உயிர்நிலை கள்ளார்க்குத்
தள்ளாது புத்தேள் உலகு.
transliteration:
Kalvaarkkuth thallum uyirnilai kallaarkkuth,
Thallaadhu puththel ulagu.
current_meaning: For those who defraud, even life in the body will fail them; for those who never defraud, even the world of the gods will not fail.
elementary_explanation: Cheaters can lose even the simple things everyone needs, like a safe life. People who stay honest are promised the biggest prize of all, like a door to heaven that will always open for them.
university_explanation: The chapter ends with an antithesis built on one verb, taḷḷu (“to fail, to reject”): life itself (uyirnilai, the soul’s stay in the body) ‘fails’ the kaḷvār, while the world of the gods (puttēḷ ulaku) ‘does not fail’ the kaḷḷār. Solomon Pappaiah reads the first clause vividly as ‘even their own life shuns the thief.’ Textual note: some online editions repeat கள்வார்க்குத் in the second line, but the antithesis requires கள்ளார்க்குத் (“to those who do not defraud”), which is the reading of Tamil Surangam, thirukkural-thamizh.org and the standard commentaries. The contrast of this-worldly collapse with heavenly reward parallels 1 Corinthians 6:10, the Chandogya Upanishad’s list of those who ‘fall,’ and the Talmud’s first question at the heavenly court.

tamil:
வாய்மை எனப்படுவது யாதெனின் யாதொன்றும்
தீமை இலாத சொலல்.
transliteration:
Vaaymai enappaduvadhu yaadhenin yaadhondrum
Theemai ilaadha solal.
current_meaning: If you ask what truthfulness really is, it is speaking words that bring no harm of any kind to anyone.
elementary_explanation: Being truthful isn’t only about not telling lies. Imagine your words are like gifts you hand to people — a truthful gift is one that never hurts anybody. So truth means saying things that are real AND that don’t cause harm.
university_explanation: Valluvar opens the chapter with a deliberately surprising definition: vaaymai is not defined by correspondence to fact (the usual Western criterion) but by its effect — speech ‘without even the least evil’ (yaadhondrum theemai ilaadha). The standard commentators (Parimelazhagar, Mu. Varadarasan, Solomon Pappaiah) all read theemai as harm to others, so truth becomes an ethical rather than merely epistemic category. This places the Kural within the broader Indian tradition that fuses satya with ahimsa, and it sets up the controversial next couplet (292) on beneficial untruth. The verse’s rhetorical form — a question answered in a definition (enappaduvadhu yaadhenin, ‘if one asks what is called…’) — marks it as the chapter’s thesis statement.

tamil:
பொய்மையும் வாய்மை யிடத்த புரைதீர்ந்த
நன்மை பயக்கும் எனின்.
transliteration:
Poymaiyum vaaymai yidaththa puraitheerndha
Nanmai payakkum enin.
current_meaning: Even a falsehood can take the place of truth, if it produces good that is wholly free of fault.
elementary_explanation: Imagine a friend is scared before a big test and asks if they look nervous. Saying “You look calm and ready!” — to help them, not to trick them for your own gain — is the kind of “kind untruth” this kural talks about. But it only counts if it does real good and hurts no one.
university_explanation: This is one of the most debated couplets in the Kural. Having defined truth by harmlessness in 291, Valluvar draws the logical consequence: a statement that is factually false but yields ‘faultless good’ (puraitheerndha nanmai) occupies ‘the place of truth’ (vaaymai idaththa). The qualifier purai theerndha — ‘with the defect removed’ — is strict: the good must be free of any taint, not merely useful to the speaker. Commentators diverge on scope: Varadarasan says such words ‘obtain the place’ of truth; Pappaiah reads it as permission to speak falsely where truth would otherwise be required. The verse places the Kural in a consequentialist line of Indian ethics (compare Krishna’s teaching in the Mahabharata) rather than the absolutism of Kant or of Buddhist precept.

tamil:
தன்நெஞ் சறிவது பொய்யற்க பொய்த்தபின்
தன்நெஞ்சே தன்னைச் சுடும்.
transliteration:
Than nenju arivadhu poyyarka poyththapin
Than nenjae thannaich chudum.
current_meaning: Do not lie about what your own heart knows to be true; once you have lied, your own heart will burn you.
elementary_explanation: Have you ever told a fib and then felt a hot, uncomfortable feeling inside, even if no one found out? That feeling is your own heart “burning” you. This kural says: don’t lie against what you know is true, because your conscience will punish you.
university_explanation: The couplet moves truthfulness from the social sphere into the interior. ‘Than nenju arivadhu’ — what one’s own heart knows — specifies a deliberate lie, one told against one’s own knowledge. The punishment is not external: ‘than nenjae thannaich chudum,’ the self’s own heart scorches the self. The repetition of than (self) three times across two lines enacts the reflexive structure of conscience. Kalaignar explicitly glosses nenju as manachaatchi, ‘conscience,’ and Pappaiah adds that the burning intensifies when the world discovers the lie — combining inner guilt with outer shame.

tamil:
உள்ளத்தாற் பொய்யா தொழுகின் உலகத்தார்
உள்ளத்து ளெல்லாம் உளன்.
transliteration:
Ullaththaal poyyaadhu ozhukin ulagaththaar
Ullaththul ellaam ulan.
current_meaning: One who lives without falsehood even in his heart will dwell in the hearts of all the people of the world.
elementary_explanation: Think of someone you completely trust — a grandparent or a teacher who never tricks you. You carry them in your heart, don’t you? This kural says that if you are honest even inside your own thoughts, everyone will keep you in their hearts too.
university_explanation: The couplet is built on an elegant chiasmus of ullam (heart/mind): one who does not lie ‘with the heart’ (ullaththaal) comes to live ‘in the hearts’ (ullaththul) of all. Truthfulness here extends past speech to conduct (ozhukin, ‘if one conducts oneself’) and even to thought — Kalaignar reads it as not even thinking falsehood. The reward is not wealth or heaven but a permanent place in human regard, which links this chapter to the preceding chapter on fame (புகழ், ch. 24). Pappaiah narrows ‘ulagaththaar’ to the noble (uyarndhavar), following the classical reading of ulagam as ‘the worthy.’

tamil:
மனத்தொடு வாய்மை மொழியின் தவத்தொடு
தானஞ்செய் வாரின் தலை.
transliteration:
Manaththodu vaaymai mozhiyin thavaththodu
Thaanam seyvaarin thalai.
current_meaning: One who speaks truth in harmony with his heart stands above those who practise both austerity and charity.
elementary_explanation: Some people do hard things to look holy, like fasting, and some give lots of gifts. This kural says that someone who simply speaks the truth from the heart, every day, is even greater than people who do both of those big things.
university_explanation: Here Valluvar ranks truthfulness above the two most prestigious religious practices of his world: thavam (tapas, ascetic austerity, the subject of chapter 27) and dhaanam (charity/gift-giving). The qualifier manaththodu — ‘together with the mind’ — is decisive: only truth that agrees with inner conviction counts, not lip-truth (Kalaignar: ‘udhattalavil indri ulamaara,’ ‘not just from the lips but from the heart’). The couplet belongs to a broad pan-Indian and wider religious critique of ritualism, in which inner integrity outweighs outer observance. Its hierarchy — truth above tapas — is stated almost verbatim in the Mahabharata’s image of truth outweighing a hundred horse-sacrifices.

tamil:
பொய்யாமை அன்ன புகழில்லை எய்யாமை
எல்லா அறமுந் தரும்.
transliteration:
Poyyaamai anna pugazhillai eyyaamai
Ellaa aramum tharum.
current_meaning: There is no fame like that of never lying; without any strain, it brings every other virtue along with it.
elementary_explanation: Being known as someone who never lies is the best reputation you can have. And it’s like a magnet — once you are truthful, other good habits, like fairness and kindness, come to you easily, without you even trying hard.
university_explanation: The couplet makes two claims: truthfulness is the supreme source of pugazh (fame, cf. ch. 24), and it ‘yields every dharma’ (ellaa aramum tharum). The pivot word eyyaamai is read in two ways: Parimelazhagar-line commentators take it as ‘without suffering/strain’ — truthfulness produces all virtue effortlessly, unlike painful austerity; Varadarasan and Pappaiah read it as ‘without one’s knowing it,’ i.e., the virtues accrue unnoticed. Either way the claim is that veracity is a generative, master virtue from which the others follow — a thesis close to the Islamic hadith that truthfulness leads to righteousness.

tamil:
பொய்யாமை பொய்யாமை ஆற்றின் அறம்பிற
செய்யாமை செய்யாமை நன்று.
transliteration:
Poyyaamai poyyaamai aatrin aram pira
Seyyaamai seyyaamai nandru.
current_meaning: If one practises truthfulness without ever failing in it, it is well even if one does no other virtuous deed.
elementary_explanation: Imagine a report card where one subject counts so much that getting it right is enough to pass everything. For Valluvar, truthfulness is that subject: if you never fail at being honest, you’re doing well even if you haven’t done any other good deeds yet.
university_explanation: A celebrated example of Valluvar’s wordplay: poyyaamai poyyaamai (literally ‘non-lying, not failing’) and seyyaamai seyyaamai (‘not doing, not doing’). The first pair means practising non-falsehood unfailingly; the second is read by most commentators (Parimelazhagar, Pappaiah) as ‘not doing [other virtues] is itself not a lack’ — truth alone suffices. Varadarasan offers a softer reading (‘practising other virtues also becomes good’), and Kalaignar reads it as truthfulness surpassing the merit of mere abstentions. The dominant reading makes veracity a sufficient condition of the good life, the strongest claim in the chapter after 300.

tamil:
புறந்தூய்மை நீரான் அமையும் அகந்தூய்மை
வாய்மையால் காணப் படும்.
transliteration:
Purandhooymai neeraan amaiyum agandhooymai
Vaaymaiyaal kaanap padum.
current_meaning: Outer purity comes from water; inner purity is seen through truthfulness.
elementary_explanation: When you get muddy, you take a bath and you’re clean on the outside. But how do you get clean on the inside? This kural says water can’t reach there — only telling the truth can wash your mind and heart.
university_explanation: The couplet sets up a clean binary: puram / agam (outer / inner), a pairing that also names the two great genres of classical Tamil poetry. Outer purity ‘is achieved’ (amaiyum) by water; inner purity ‘is seen / made manifest’ (kaanappadum) by truthfulness — truth both produces and reveals a clean mind. This is a pointed comment on ritual bathing (neeraadal) in holy waters. Textual note: several popular web editions print the first word as ‘புறள்தூய்மை’; the grammatically regular form ‘புறந்தூய்மை’ (puram + thooymai), used here, is attested in other editions and fits the parallel with அகந்தூய்மை.

tamil:
எல்லா விளக்கும் விளக்கல்ல சான்றோர்க்குப்
பொய்யா விளக்கே விளக்கு.
transliteration:
Ellaa vilakkum vilakkalla saandrorkkup
Poyyaa vilakke vilakku.
current_meaning: Not every lamp is a true lamp; for the wise, the lamp of truthfulness alone is the real lamp.
elementary_explanation: A flashlight helps you see in a dark room. But what helps you see the right thing to do when you are confused inside? This kural says truthfulness is that special inner flashlight — and for wise people, it’s the only lamp that really matters.
university_explanation: The couplet repeats vilakku (lamp) four times, playing on its meanings: ordinary lamps dispel outer darkness, but ‘the lamp that does not lie’ (poyyaa vilakku) dispels inner darkness. Varadarasan’s gloss adds the parenthetical contrast explicitly: lamps that remove darkness outside versus the lamp of non-falsehood that removes darkness within. Saandror — the noble, the wise — is a key Kural term (cf. ch. 99, Saandraanmai), suggesting truthfulness is the defining light of the fully mature person. The truth-as-light metaphor is among the most widely shared images across religious traditions.

tamil:
யாமெய்யாக் கண்டவற்றுள் இல்லை எனைத்தொன்றும்
வாய்மையின் நல்ல பிற.
transliteration:
Yaam meyyaak kandavatrul illai enaiththondrum
Vaaymaiyin nalla pira.
current_meaning: Among all the things we have found to be truly real and good, there is nothing, in any way, better than truthfulness.
elementary_explanation: Imagine you searched the whole world and all the best books for the most precious treasure. Valluvar says he did that kind of search — and the greatest treasure he found was simply telling the truth.
university_explanation: The chapter closes with a personal verdict — one of the rare places Valluvar speaks in the first person (yaam, ‘we’). ‘Meyyaak kandavai’ means ‘things seen/found as real,’ and there is a deliberate play between mey (reality, truth) and vaaymai (truthful speech): among all that is mey, nothing surpasses vaaymai. Pappaiah reads kandavai as ‘the books I have examined,’ making this a survey of all moral literature; Kalaignar takes it as the conclusion of research into what is true. Either way, the couplet sets veracity at the summit of all virtues, bringing the chapter full circle from its opening definition.
